docs.title: Rust Programming: From Zero to Useful
docs.text: Learn Rust from first principles to a small command-line application.

docs.title: Course target
docs.text: By the end, you will be able to write, test, and package small Rust programs with confidence.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
This course is for programmers who are new to Rust. You should be comfortable with a terminal and basic programming ideas such as variables, functions, and conditionals. Install the stable Rust toolchain with rustup before starting.

Start with Module 0: First lesson, then use the roadmap and syllabus to plan the track.

docs.title: Final goal
docs.text:
Build a tested command-line task tracker while learning Rust's ownership model, types, error handling, and project tooling.

Milestone Modules Outcome Foundation 0–2 Compile Rust, use core types, and understand ownership. Application 3–6 Model data, use traits, handle errors, test projects, and apply Rust software design principles. Capstone 7 Build and test a persistent command-line task tracker. Advanced 8–9 Use closures, advanced lifetimes, and smart pointers. Concurrent programs 10–11 Build threaded and async applications. Systems practice 12–13 Measure performance and define safe unsafe/FFI boundaries.

docs.title: Recommended sequence
docs.text:
1. Start with Module 0 and compile every example locally.
  2. Learn basic types and collections in Module 1, then ownership and borrowing in Module 2.
  3. Learn structs and traits before advanced lifetime and shared-ownership patterns.
  4. Complete Modules 3–6 before the Module 7 capstone; apply Module 6 SOLID, composition, and testable design guidance in the project.
  5. Continue to Modules 8–13 using the prerequisites in the syllabus.

Modules 0–1 are available. Module 2 Topics 1–7 are published, while Topic 8 and Module 3 Topics 1–2 are published; the remaining Module 3 topics and Modules 4–13 are planned. Module 0 packaging, workspace, and embedded extensions are optional for the main learning path.

docs.title: Syllabus
docs.text: This syllabus moves from toolchain basics to ownership, then into application design and a tested command-line capstone. Modules 0–1 are available; Module 2 is partially implemented (Topics 1–7 are published, Topic 8 is planned). All other modules below are planned; Module 3 Topics 1–2 are published. Follow the numbered order; later modules name any additional prerequisites. A topic listed here is not necessarily a published lesson.

docs.title: 0. Hello, Rust and tooling
docs.text:
• Install Rust and understand rustup, rustc, Cargo, rustfmt, Clippy, and rust-analyzer.
  • Build, run, format, check, test, and package a Hello World application.
  • Optional extensions: Debian packaging, compiler outputs, Cargo workspaces, and Raspberry Pi Pico cross-compilation. These are not prerequisites for Module 1.

Completion goal: build, run, format, and check a Hello World application.

docs.title: 1. Rust fundamentals
docs.text:
All eight topics are published: an overview, bindings, scalar types, collections, functions, conditions, loops, and Cargo/testing practice. Follow the topic index in numbered order.

  • Variables, mutability, scalar and compound types.
  • Functions, expressions, control flow, and pattern basics.
  • Arrays, tuples, String, and Vec<T>; loops, indexing, and basic methods.
  • Structuring small programs with Cargo.
  • Testing simple behavior and reading compiler feedback.

Completion goal: write and test a function that summarizes a list of numbers.

docs.title: 2. Ownership and borrowing
docs.text:
• Values, variables, scope, stack and heap storage.
  • Move semantics, Copy, and Clone.
  • Shared and mutable borrowing.
  • Collections, iterators, slices, and API boundaries.
  • Introductory lifetimes: references must remain valid while used (planned Topic 8).
  • Advanced ownership continues in Modules 8–10 and 13 after structs and traits.
  • Hands-on review: ownership tracing, move repair, snapshots, borrowed iteration, numeric/text slices, and an advanced pipeline combining borrowing with ownership transfer.

Completion goal: implement functions that read and update caller-owned data without unnecessary clones, and explain a borrow-checker diagnostic.

docs.title: 3. Structs, enums, and data modeling — Topics 1–2 published
docs.text:
• Define structs and implement methods with impl blocks.
  • Use associated functions and model domain data.
  • Define enums and use match, if let, and pattern matching.
  • Represent missing values with Option<T>.
  • Model operation outcomes with Result<T, E>.

Completion goal: model a task with a struct, status enum, and methods, then demonstrate success, a missing task with Option, and a rejected operation with Result.

docs.title: 4. Traits and generics — planned
docs.text:
• Define and implement traits.
  • Use generic functions, generic types, and trait bounds.
  • Derive common traits such as Debug, Clone, and Default.
  • Compare trait bounds, impl Trait, and dyn Trait at an introductory level.

Completion goal: implement one trait for two types and use both through a generic function.

docs.title: 5. Error handling, modules, and testing — planned
docs.text:
• Distinguish recoverable errors from panics and interpret Result.
  • Create custom error types and propagate errors with ?.
  • Organize modules, visibility, Cargo targets, and unit/integration tests.
  • Read files and test malformed input and missing files.

Completion goal: build a library plus binary that loads data and reports errors without using unwrap() for expected failures.

docs.title: 6. Rust software design and patterns — planned
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: Modules 3–5.
  • Encapsulation: private fields, validated constructors, and types that prevent invalid states.
  • Apply SOLID pragmatically: focused responsibilities, useful extension points, trait behavioral contracts, small interfaces, and dependency inversion.
  • Compose structs, enums, and traits; inject dependencies through constructors and function parameters.
  • Design public APIs with deliberate ownership, borrowed parameters, meaningful errors, and minimal exposed implementation details.
  • Use Builder, Strategy, Adapter, State, and Newtype patterns when concrete requirements justify them; compare enum-based and trait-based designs.
  • Separate core application logic from CLI input, file storage, networking, and hardware; refactor incrementally with tests.

Completion goal: build a task service with a small storage trait, an in-memory implementation for tests, and a file implementation. Test the same behavioral contract for both, and explain why each abstraction is needed.

docs.title: 7. Command-line task tracker capstone — planned
docs.text:
• Parse command-line commands and arguments.
  • Combine structs, enums, ownership, borrowing, and error handling.
  • Persist tasks to a file using a stable data format.
  • Split the application into focused Cargo modules.
  • Apply Module 6 design principles to separate task logic from CLI and storage.
  • Add unit tests, integration tests, and useful user-facing errors.

Completion goal: provide add, list, complete, and delete commands; preserve tasks across runs; test valid commands, invalid input, and persistence failures.

docs.title: 8. Closures and advanced iterators — planned
docs.text: • Prerequisites: Modules 2–5.

docs.title: Planned topic sequence
docs.text:
1. Closures and captures: closure syntax, borrowing captures, move, and the Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce traits.
  2. Iterator fundamentals and laziness: Iterator, next(), and why adapters do no work until the iterator is consumed. Apply the same methods to ranges and collection iterators.
  3. Transforming and filtering: map() changes each yielded value; filter() keeps values matching a predicate.
  4. Selecting and numbering: take() limits the number of items, skip() omits initial items, and enumerate() pairs items with zero-based positions. Revisit rev() and step_by() and explore how adapter order changes results.
  5. Consuming results: sum(), count(), and collect(), including the type annotations needed to choose a sum type or output collection.
  6. Ownership through pipelines: compare iter(), iter_mut(), and into_iter() when closures read, change, or take ownership of elements.
  7. Custom iterators and practice: implement Iterator for a small type, then build and test a filtering pipeline with empty and no-match cases.

Completion goal: build and test a filtering pipeline with a closure whose capture mode you can explain.

docs.title: 9. Advanced lifetimes and smart pointers — planned
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: Modules 3–5 and 8.
  • Borrowed structs, lifetime annotations, elision, and method receivers.
  • Ownership in Option and Result; as_ref and as_mut.
  • Box, Rc, and RefCell; interior mutability and ownership design.

Completion goal: compare owned and borrowed representations, and demonstrate shared ownership with checked interior mutation.

docs.title: 10. Threads and concurrency — planned
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: Modules 8–9.
  • Thread spawning, joining, channels, Send, and Sync.
  • Arc, Mutex, and RwLock; lock scope and deadlock avoidance.

Completion goal: implement a threaded worker example and test that all results are collected and all threads terminate.

docs.title: 11. Async Rust — planned
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: Modules 8–10.
  • Futures, async/.await, executors, and task ownership.
  • Async I/O, cancellation, timeouts, and avoiding blocking work in async tasks.

Completion goal: implement concurrent I/O with explicit timeout and error handling.

docs.title: 12. Performance and profiling — planned
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: Modules 7–9; Modules 10–11 for concurrent examples.
  • Release builds, benchmarks, profiling, allocation costs, and cloning costs.
  • Measure changes while preserving behavior and tests.

Completion goal: benchmark a working program, identify one bottleneck, and compare performance before and after a tested improvement.

docs.title: 13. Unsafe Rust and FFI — planned
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: Modules 9–12.
  • Raw pointers, safety contracts, and small safe interfaces around unsafe code.
  • C interoperability, ABI boundaries, and allocation ownership across FFI.
  • Self-referential designs and pinning, revisiting futures from Module 11.

Completion goal: wrap a small FFI call with documented ownership and safety requirements and tests for its safe interface.

docs.title: Module 0: Hello, Rust and tooling
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to install Rust and build, run, format, and check a Hello World application.

  • Install and understand the Rust toolchain.
  • Create and run a Cargo application.
  • Explore optional packaging, compiler-output, workspace, and embedded workflows.

Prerequisites: a terminal and basic programming familiarity. All five topics are published. Complete Topic 1 for the main course; Topics 2–5 are optional extensions and are not prerequisites for Module 1.

docs.title: 1. Set up Rust and build Hello World
docs.text:
• Install stable Rust with rustup.
  • Understand rustc, Cargo, formatting, linting, and editor tools.
  • Create, build, run, check, test, and package a small application.

Start with Setup and Hello World.

docs.title: 2. From source to DEB — optional
docs.text:
• Build an optimized release binary.
  • Package an application as a Debian .deb file.
  • Install and remove the package on Debian or Ubuntu.

After Topic 1, explore From source to DEB.

docs.title: 3. Linux compiler output — optional
docs.text:
• Locate Cargo's generated files on Linux.
  • Compare debug and release output.
  • Inspect executable and library artifacts.

After Topic 1, explore Linux compiler output.

docs.title: 4. Cargo workspace with a binary and library — optional
docs.text:
• Group related packages under a workspace manifest.
  • Separate an executable from reusable library code.
  • Organize library modules and call them from the executable.

After Topic 1, explore Cargo workspaces.

docs.title: 5. Cross-compile for Raspberry Pi Pico — optional
docs.text:
• Build firmware for the RP2040 target.
  • Flash through the USB bootloader and print over USB serial.
  • Understand the role of a debug probe.

After Topic 1, explore Raspberry Pi Pico cross-compilation. Follow that lesson's hardware and tool prerequisites.

docs.title: Completion and next module
docs.text:
You are ready to continue when you can run Hello World and explain which commands build, check, and format it.

Next: Module 1: Rust fundamentals.

docs.title: Topic 1: Set up Rust and build Hello World
By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Install the stable Rust toolchain with rustup.
  • Explain the jobs of rustup, rustc, and Cargo.
  • Build, run, format, check, and package a small application.

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Rust programs start at a function named main. The println! macro writes a line of text to the terminal. Rust checks the program before running it, so mistakes are reported early by the compiler.

flowchart LR
  A[main function] --> B[println! macro]
  B --> C[Compiled binary]

docs.title: Install the toolchain
docs.text:
The recommended installer is rustup. On Linux, macOS, or WSL, run:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

Accept the default stable toolchain, then open a new terminal so the Cargo bin directory is on your PATH. On Windows, download and run rustup-init.exe from the official installation page. Windows builds may also need the Visual Studio C++ build tools.

Verify the installation:

rustup show
rustc --version
cargo --version

Keep the stable toolchain current with rustup update. If a command is not found after installation, restart the terminal and check that $HOME/.cargo/bin is on PATH.

docs.title: The important commands
docs.text:
Command Job rustup Installs and selects Rust toolchains and components. rustc Compiles a Rust source file directly. cargo Creates, builds, runs, tests, documents, and packages projects. rustfmt Formats Rust source consistently. clippy Finds common mistakes and non-idiomatic Rust. rustdoc Generates API documentation from Rust comments. rust-analyzer Gives editor features such as completion and diagnostics.

The standard stable installation includes Cargo, rustfmt, and Clippy. If a component is missing, install it explicitly:

rustup component add rustfmt clippy
rustup component add rust-src  # useful for rust-analyzer

Most editors install or bundle rust-analyzer; VS Code uses the official extension. The compiler tools work independently of any editor.

docs.title: Create a Hello World application
docs.text:
Cargo keeps the source layout and build metadata together. From the repository root, create a new application in a temporary directory:

cargo new /tmp/hello-rust
cd /tmp/hello-rust

Cargo creates Cargo.toml and src/main.rs. Replace src/main.rs with:

fn main() {
    println!("Hello, Rust!");
}

docs.title: Build, run, and package it
docs.text:
Run these commands inside /tmp/hello-rust:

cargo check                 # type-check quickly without creating a binary
cargo build                 # debug build in target/debug/
cargo run                   # build if needed, then run the binary
cargo run -- Rust           # pass Rust as an argument to the binary
cargo build --release       # optimized build in target/release/
cargo test                  # run tests, when the project has tests
cargo doc --open            # build and open local API documentation
cargo package --allow-dirty # validate the package archive locally

For this application, the release binary is target/release/hello-rust on Linux and macOS, or target/release/hello-rust.exe on Windows. cargo package creates a crate archive for distribution and checks that the package can be published. It does not upload anything. Use cargo publish only when you intend to publish a crate to crates.io.

docs.title: Format and lint before sharing
docs.text:
cargo fmt                 # format the whole project
cargo fmt -- --check      # fail if formatting would change files
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

rustfmt handles layout. Clippy provides advice about correctness, performance, and idiomatic style. Treat warnings as errors in CI when the project is ready for that policy.

The commands above are the standard Rust workflow: check, format, lint, test, build, then create a release artifact.

docs.title: Run the course example
docs.text:
The repository also contains a Cargo version of Hello World:

cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml

Expected output:

Hello, Rust!

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Change the message in examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/src/main.rs, run cargo fmt, and use cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml to see the result.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
1. Which command manages Rust toolchains?
  2. Which command runs the current Cargo package?
  3. Which command formats Rust source code?

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Build a Rust release binary with Cargo.
  • Package it as a Debian .deb file.
  • Install and remove the package on Debian or Ubuntu.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
cargo-deb reads your Cargo project, builds the release binary, and places it inside a Debian package with metadata from Cargo.toml.

flowchart LR
  S[Rust source] --> C[Cargo build]
  C --> P[cargo-deb]
  P --> D[.deb package]
  D --> I[apt install]

This lesson assumes a binary Cargo project with a Cargo.toml file and a src/main.rs entry point.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the project
docs.text:
From the project root, check, format, lint, and test before packaging:

cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test
cargo build --release

The release binary is written to target/release/<binary-name>.

docs.title: 2. Install the Debian packager
docs.text:
Install the Cargo subcommand once:

cargo install cargo-deb

If installation reports that Rust is too old, update the Rust toolchain first:

rustup update

docs.title: 3. Add package metadata
docs.text:
A basic binary can be packaged without extra configuration. Add metadata when you want a maintainer, section, or explicit runtime dependencies:

[package.metadata.deb]
maintainer = "Your Name <you@example.com>"
section = "utils"
priority = "optional"
depends = "$auto"

The package name and version come from the [package] section:

[package]
name = "hello-rust"
version = "0.1.0"

docs.title: 4. Create the .deb file
docs.text:
Run this from the directory containing Cargo.toml:

cargo deb

The result is written to target/debian/. Its filename contains the package name, version, Debian revision, and architecture, for example:

target/debian/hello-rust_0.1.0-1_amd64.deb

To package the course Hello World project from the repository root:

cargo deb \
  --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/hello-world/Cargo.toml

docs.title: 5. Inspect and install it
docs.text:
Inspect the archive before installing it:

dpkg-deb --info target/debian/hello-rust_*.deb
dpkg-deb --contents target/debian/hello-rust_*.deb

Install it locally with apt, which can resolve package dependencies:

sudo apt install ./target/debian/hello-rust_*.deb

Run the installed program:

hello-rust

Remove it later with:

sudo apt remove hello-rust

docs.title: Architecture matters
docs.text:
A .deb is built for a target architecture. Check the architecture of the current machine with:

dpkg --print-architecture

For a specific Rust target, install the target toolchain and pass it to cargo-deb:

rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
cargo deb --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

Cross-compilation may also require a linker and system libraries for the target architecture.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Which command creates the Debian package?

cargo publish cargo deb rustc --deb Check answer

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The repeatable release path is:

cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo test
cargo deb
sudo apt install ./target/debian/*.deb

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Find the important files produced by Cargo on Linux.
  • Tell debug output from release output.
  • Inspect a Rust executable with standard Linux tools.

docs.title: A small demo project
docs.text:
The demo contains one binary and one library target:

linux-compiler-output/
├── Cargo.toml
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs
    └── main.rs

Cargo discovers src/main.rs as the executable target and src/lib.rs as the library target.

Build it from the repository root:

cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml --release

Run it:

cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml

Expected output:

Hello from a Linux Rust binary
2 + 3 = 5

docs.title: What Cargo creates
docs.text:
Cargo puts compiler output in target/ by default. The profile directory separates normal development builds from optimized release builds:

Path Meaning target/debug/ Development build with fast compilation and debug information. target/release/ Optimized build intended for distribution. target/debug/<name> Debug executable. target/release/<name> Release executable. target/debug/deps/ Dependency and intermediate artifacts. target/debug/incremental/ Incremental compiler cache. target/doc/ Output from cargo doc. target/package/ Output from cargo package.

The exact contents of deps/, incremental/, and build-script directories are compiler internals. Do not copy them to a target machine.

docs.title: Common file types
docs.text:
File Meaning No extension on Linux Usually an executable binary. .rlib Rust library artifact used by the Rust compiler. .rmeta Rust metadata used during compilation. .so Dynamic shared library on Linux. .d Dependency information used to know when to rebuild. .o Object file used before final linking.

For normal application deployment, copy only the release executable or the final library package. The .rlib, .rmeta, .d, and .o files are not application deliverables.

docs.title: check versus build
docs.text:
cargo check --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml

cargo check runs the compiler's analysis without producing a final linked executable. It is fast and useful while editing. cargo build continues to link the final binary into target/debug/.

docs.title: Inspect the Linux executable
docs.text:
Use find to locate final binaries:

find examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target \
  -maxdepth 3 -type f -executable -print

Use file to identify the binary format and architecture:

file examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target/release/linux-compiler-output

On a typical 64-bit Linux host, the output includes ELF 64-bit and the machine architecture.

Use ldd to view dynamically linked system libraries:

ldd examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target/release/linux-compiler-output

Use readelf to inspect the ELF header without executing the program:

readelf -h examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/target/release/linux-compiler-output

These commands inspect the final executable. They do not replace cargo build and should not be used to edit compiler output.

docs.title: The compiler pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  A[src/main.rs] --> B[rustc analysis]
  B --> C[object files and metadata]
  C --> D[Linux linker]
  D --> E[target/release/binary]

Cargo coordinates the process, rustc compiles Rust code, and the Linux linker combines object files and libraries into the final ELF executable.

docs.title: Clean and rebuild
docs.text:
cargo clean --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/linux-compiler-output/Cargo.toml --release

cargo clean removes generated build artifacts. It does not remove source files or Cargo.toml.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Where does cargo build --release place the final binary?

target/debug/ target/release/ src/release/ Check answer

docs.title: Cargo workspace with a binary and library
By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Create a workspace containing an executable and a library package.
  • Split library code into two modules.
  • Import and call library functions from the executable.

docs.title: Workspace layout
docs.text:
A workspace groups related Cargo packages under one root manifest. In this example, app is the executable and toolkit is the library:

cargo-workspace/
├── Cargo.toml
├── app/
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src/main.rs
└── toolkit/
    ├── Cargo.toml
    └── src/
        ├── lib.rs
        ├── greetings.rs
        └── numbers.rs

The root Cargo.toml lists both packages:

[workspace]
members = ["app", "toolkit"]
resolver = "2"

The workspace root does not need its own src/ directory.

docs.title: The library package
docs.text:
toolkit/Cargo.toml identifies the library package:

[package]
name = "toolkit"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

Declare the two modules in toolkit/src/lib.rs and re-export their public functions:

pub mod greetings;
pub mod numbers;

The first module, toolkit/src/greetings.rs, contains a greeting function:

pub fn hello(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

The second module, toolkit/src/numbers.rs, contains a calculation:

pub fn add(left: i32, right: i32) -> i32 {
    left + right
}

pub makes the modules and functions available outside the library crate.

docs.title: The executable package
docs.text:
Declare the library as a path dependency in app/Cargo.toml:

[package]
name = "app"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
toolkit = { path = "../toolkit" }

The executable imports both modules and calls one function from each:

use toolkit::{greetings, numbers};

fn main() {
    println!("{}", greetings::hello("workspace"));
    println!("2 + 3 = {}", numbers::add(2, 3));
}

Expected output:

Hello, workspace!
2 + 3 = 5

The dependency graph is:

flowchart LR
  W[Workspace] --> A[app binary]
  A --> T[toolkit library]
  T --> G[greetings module]
  T --> N[numbers module]

docs.title: Build and run the workspace
docs.text:
Run these commands from the workspace root:

cargo check
cargo test
cargo run -p app
cargo build --release -p app

Cargo builds the library before linking the executable. The release executable is written to target/release/app on Linux.

You can also run the package by manifest path from the repository root:

cargo run --manifest-path examples/00-first-lesson/cargo-workspace/app/Cargo.toml

Cargo finds the workspace root by following the package's parent directories.

docs.title: Tests belong next to the code they verify
docs.text:
The demo puts unit tests in the library modules:

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::add;

    #[test]
    fn adds_two_numbers() {
        assert_eq!(add(2, 3), 5);
    }
}

Run all workspace tests with:

cargo test

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
How does the executable use the local library package?

By copying lib.rs into main.rs By publishing the library first By declaring a path dependency in app/Cargo.toml Check answer

docs.title: Cross-compile Rust for a Raspberry Pi Pico
By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Build Rust firmware for the RP2040 Cortex-M0+ processor.
  • Send Hello, Pico! to a computer over USB serial.
  • Flash the firmware through the Pico USB bootloader.
  • Understand how a debug probe enables breakpoints and stepping.

docs.title: What changes on a Pico?
docs.text:
A Linux Rust program targets the host operating system. Pico firmware is bare-metal code, so it needs a different target, a board memory layout, a startup runtime, and a flashing method.

The RP2040 uses two Cortex-M0+ cores. Rust targets it with thumbv6m-none-eabi.

flowchart LR
  A[Rust source] --> B[rustc for thumbv6m-none-eabi]
  B --> C[ARM ELF firmware]
  C --> D[UF2 or SWD flash]
  D --> E[RP2040 Pico]
  E --> F[USB CDC serial output]

The rp-pico board-support package configures the Pico pins and RP2040 HAL. The usb-device and usbd-serial crates expose a USB CDC-ACM serial port.

docs.title: Install the embedded toolchain
docs.text:
rustup target add thumbv6m-none-eabi
cargo install --locked elf2uf2-rs

elf2uf2-rs converts the ARM ELF output to UF2 and can copy it to the mounted RPI-RP2 bootloader drive. The demo uses rust-lld, so a separate ARM GCC compiler is not required.

docs.title: Project configuration
docs.text:
The demo's .cargo/config.toml selects the cross target and linker script:

[build]
target = "thumbv6m-none-eabi"

[target.thumbv6m-none-eabi]
linker = "rust-lld"
runner = "elf2uf2-rs -d"
rustflags = [
    "-C", "link-arg=--nmagic",
    "-C", "link-arg=-Tlink.x",
]

memory.x describes the Pico's flash and RAM layout. Keeping it beside Cargo.toml lets the linker use the board's memory map directly.

docs.title: USB Hello Pico application
docs.text:
The application is #![no_std] and #![no_main]. It initializes the RP2040 clocks, creates a USB CDC serial class, and writes a greeting while polling USB.

// A bare-metal firmware has no operating system or standard library.
#![no_std]
// The Cortex-M runtime supplies the entry point instead of a normal `main` ABI.
#![no_main]

// Halt the processor if an unrecoverable panic occurs.
use panic_halt as _;
// `entry` marks the reset entry point, `hal` provides board drivers, and `pac`
// exposes the RP2040 peripheral registers.
use rp_pico::{entry, hal, pac};
// USB device traits and the CDC serial class used by the host terminal.
use usb_device::{class_prelude::*, prelude::*};
use usbd_serial::SerialPort;

// Firmware entry points never return, so the function returns the never type.
#[entry]
fn main() -> ! {
    // Take ownership of the device peripherals exactly once after reset.
    let mut peripherals = pac::Peripherals::take().unwrap();
    // The watchdog is required while the RP2040 clocks are configured.
    let mut watchdog = hal::Watchdog::new(peripherals.WATCHDOG);

    // Configure the Pico oscillator, system PLL, and USB PLL.
    let clocks = hal::clocks::init_clocks_and_plls(
        rp_pico::XOSC_CRYSTAL_FREQ,
        peripherals.XOSC,
        peripherals.CLOCKS,
        peripherals.PLL_SYS,
        peripherals.PLL_USB,
        &mut peripherals.RESETS,
        &mut watchdog,
    )
    .ok()
    .unwrap();

    // Create the USB bus that owns the RP2040 USB peripheral and its DPRAM.
    let usb_bus = UsbBusAllocator::new(hal::usb::UsbBus::new(
        peripherals.USBCTRL_REGS,
        peripherals.USBCTRL_DPRAM,
        clocks.usb_clock,
        true,
        &mut peripherals.RESETS,
    ));

    // Add a USB CDC-ACM serial interface to the bus.
    let mut serial = SerialPort::new(&usb_bus);
    // Describe the USB device to the host computer.
    let mut usb_device = UsbDeviceBuilder::new(&usb_bus, UsbVidPid(0x16c0, 0x27dd))
        .strings(&[StringDescriptors::default().product("Hello Pico")])
        .unwrap()
        .build();

    loop {
        // Poll services USB enumeration and transfer events.
        if usb_device.poll(&mut [&mut serial]) {
            // The demo ignores WouldBlock to keep the example small.
            let _ = serial.write(b"Hello from Pico!\r\n");
        }
    }
}

The same code is in the demo's src/main.rs.

docs.title: What happens at startup?
docs.text:
1. #![no_std] removes the operating-system-dependent Rust standard library.
  2. #[entry] tells cortex-m-rt which function runs after reset.
  3. pac::Peripherals::take() gives the firmware unique access to hardware registers.
  4. The watchdog and PLL setup produce the system and USB clocks.
  5. UsbBus owns the RP2040 USB peripheral and its packet memory.
  6. SerialPort creates a USB CDC-ACM interface that Linux exposes as a serial device such as /dev/ttyACM0.
  7. poll keeps USB enumeration and transfers moving. When it reports an event, the example writes Hello from Pico! to the serial endpoint.

The current demo writes on every successful poll event, so a terminal may show the greeting repeatedly while USB traffic is active. That is intentional for a small polling demonstration. A production logger would handle WouldBlock, buffer messages, and usually rate-limit output.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
rp2040-hello-pico/
├── .cargo/
│   └── config.toml
├── src/
│   └── main.rs
├── Cargo.toml
├── Cargo.lock
├── memory.x
├── .gitignore
└── target/
File or directory Role Cargo.toml Names the firmware package and declares Rust dependencies. Cargo.lock Records the exact dependency versions used for a reproducible build. .cargo/config.toml Selects thumbv6m-none-eabi, linker flags, and the flash runner. src/main.rs Contains the no_std firmware entry point and USB serial loop. memory.x Defines the RP2040 flash, boot2, and RAM addresses for the linker. .gitignore Keeps generated target/ files out of version control. target/ Generated compiler output. It is not source code and should not be committed.

The package is named pico_hellp to match the working demo. The rp-pico dependency supplies the board support package, usb-device supplies the USB device framework, usbd-serial supplies the CDC serial class, and panic-halt stops the CPU if an unrecoverable panic occurs.

docs.title: Build the firmware
docs.text:
From the repository root, enter the demo directory first so Cargo discovers the embedded .cargo/config.toml:

cd examples/00-first-lesson/rp2040-hello-pico
cargo check
cargo build --release

The final ELF is written under:

target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico_hellp

docs.title: Flash over USB bootloader
docs.text:
1. Hold the Pico's BOOTSEL button.
  2. Connect the Pico to USB.
  3. Release BOOTSEL after the RPI-RP2 drive appears.
  4. Run:
cargo run --release

The configured elf2uf2-rs -d runner converts and copies the firmware. You can also create a UF2 file without flashing it:

elf2uf2-rs target/thumbv6m-none-eabi/release/pico_hellp hello-pico.uf2

Copy hello-pico.uf2 to the mounted RPI-RP2 drive, then wait for the Pico to reboot.

docs.title: Read the USB output
docs.text:
After the firmware boots, a new USB serial device should appear. On Linux it is often /dev/ttyACM0:

ls /dev/ttyACM*
screen /dev/ttyACM0 115200

The USB CDC connection does not use a physical baud rate, so 115200 is only a conventional terminal setting. Press Ctrl-A, then K to exit screen.

docs.title: Debugging the Pico
docs.text:
Yes, but USB serial output is logging, not source-level debugging. For breakpoints, stepping, register inspection, and memory inspection, use SWD with a debug probe such as a Raspberry Pi Debug Probe, J-Link, or a second Pico flashed with CMSIS-DAP debug-probe firmware.

Connect SWCLK, SWDIO, and GND from the probe to the target Pico. Install probe-rs and list the probe:

cargo install --locked probe-rs-tools
probe-rs list

Temporarily change the runner to:

runner = "probe-rs run --chip RP2040"

Then flash and run through SWD:

cargo run

The probe-rs VS Code extension can provide breakpoints and stepping. Keep debug information enabled in the debug profile so source lines map correctly.

docs.title: Module 1: Rust fundamentals
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to write and test a small Rust program that summarizes a list of numbers.

  • Declare values and choose suitable types.
  • Work with collections and text.
  • Write functions, decisions, and loops.
  • Run a Cargo project, test behavior, and repair compiler errors.

Prerequisite: Module 0 setup and Hello World. All eight topics are published. Follow the numbered order, then complete the number-summary exercise in Topic 8 before moving to Module 2.

docs.text:
• Understand the edit, compile, and run cycle.
  • Run and change a small program.
  • Preview the module learning path.

Start with Topic 1: Fundamentals overview.

docs.title: 2. Variables, mutability, and shadowing
docs.text:
• Declare bindings with let and distinguish immutable and mutable bindings.
  • Use shadowing to introduce a new binding, including one of a different type.
  • Define typed constants with const.

Continue with Topic 2: Variables, mutability, and shadowing.

docs.title: 3. Scalar types and operators
docs.text:

  • Understand type inference, explicit annotations, and integer division.
  • Recognize overflow and use comparisons and Boolean operators.

Continue with Topic 3: Scalar types and operators.

docs.text:
• Choose fixed-size arrays, tuples, or growable vectors.
  • Index sequences, check lengths, and use basic methods.
  • Destructure tuples and distinguish String from borrowed text.
  • Recognize UTF-8 byte lengths and why strings cannot be indexed by integer.

Continue with Topic 4: Arrays, tuples, strings, and vectors.

docs.title: 5. Functions, statements, and expressions
docs.text:
• Define typed parameters and return values.
  • Return a tail expression or use an early return.
  • Explain how a semicolon affects an expression and the unit type ().

Continue with Topic 5: Functions, statements, and expressions.

docs.title: 6. Conditions and pattern basics
docs.text:
• Use if and else for decisions and as expressions.
  • Choose branches with match.
  • Cover remaining values with a wildcard pattern.

Continue with Topic 6: Conditions and pattern basics.

docs.title: 7. Loops and ranges
docs.text:
• Iterate with for and distinguish exclusive and inclusive ranges.
    • Choose a step size with step_by().
    • Count in reverse with rev().
  • Repeat with while and loop.
  • Use break, continue, and values returned by a loop.

Continue with Topic 7: Loops and ranges.

docs.title: 8. Cargo practice, tests, and compiler feedback
docs.text:

  • Add a function and test typical and empty inputs.
  • Distinguish compiler errors from failed assertions and repair both.

Continue with Topic 8: Cargo practice, tests, and compiler feedback.

docs.title: From source to a running program
docs.text:
Rust source describes the steps a program should perform. The compiler checks that source and creates an executable; running the executable performs those steps. Cargo automates the build and run workflow for projects.

flowchart LR
    A[Edit Rust source] --> B[Compile and check types]
    B --> C[Run executable]
    C --> D[Observe output]

When does a compiler type error need to be fixed?

Before an executable can be built successfully Only after the executable exits Only when writing tests Check answer

docs.title: Topic 2: Variables, mutability, and shadowing
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to

  • Declare immutable and mutable bindings.
  • Distinguish mutation from shadowing.
  • Define a typed constant.

Prerequisite: Topic 1: Fundamentals overview.

docs.title: Names and change
docs.text:
A variable gives a value a name. Rust infers many types, but function interfaces and ambiguous values need explicit types. A binding is immutable by default.

let mut attempts: u8 = 2;
attempts += 1;             // Mutation requires mut.
let attempts = attempts.to_string(); // Shadowing creates a new binding.
println!("{attempts}");

Shadowing with another let can change the type; assigning to an existing mut binding cannot change its type. Use const LIMIT: usize = 10; for a named constant whose value is computed at compile time.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
Why is the final let attempts = attempts.to_string() allowed?

mut permits any type change A new binding shadows the old one All variables are strings internally Check answer

A constant needs an explicit type and a compile-time value. For example, const LIMIT: usize = 10; does not create a mutable counter.

Can assigning to a mutable integer binding change its type to text?

Yes, mut allows any type No, assignment preserves the binding’s type Only if the text contains digits Check answer

docs.title: Runnable example
docs.text:
fn main() {
    const LIMIT: usize = 10;
    let mut attempts: usize = 2;
    attempts += 1;
    assert_eq!(attempts, 3);
    assert!(attempts < LIMIT);
    let attempts = attempts.to_string();
    assert_eq!(attempts, "3");
    println!("attempts: {attempts}, limit: {LIMIT}");
}

Run from the repository root:

rustc examples/01-fundamentals/02-variables-mutability-shadowing/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-fundamentals-2
/tmp/rust-fundamentals-2

Expected output:

attempts: 3, limit: 10

docs.text: Start the counter at 4, increase it by 2, and update the assertions. Remove mut, read the error, then restore it. Explain why shadowing still needs a new let even when the original binding is mutable.

docs.text:
Which choice creates a new binding?

docs.title: Topic 3: Scalar types and operators
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to

  • Choose scalar types and use type annotations.
  • Predict integer and floating-point division.
  • Use arithmetic, comparisons, and Boolean operators.

Prerequisite: Topic 2: Variables, mutability, and shadowing.

docs.title: Choose a type for the value
docs.text:
Rust infers many local types from their values and uses. An annotation such as let temperature: f64 = 21.5; makes the choice explicit. Function parameters require declared types. Single quotes denote a char, such as 'λ'; double quotes denote text.

Type Meaning Example i32 Signed 32-bit integer -12 u8 Unsigned 8-bit integer 255 usize Unsigned type used for lengths and indexes values.len() f64 Floating-point number 21.5 bool Boolean true char Unicode scalar value 'λ'

Integer division truncates toward zero: 5 / 2 is 2, while 5.0 / 2.0 is 2.5. Choose types to fit the data; integer overflow is not automatic promotion to a larger type.

What is the value of integer division 5 / 2?

2 2.5 3 Check answer

docs.title: Arithmetic and Boolean operators
docs.text:
Use +, -, *, /, and % for arithmetic and remainder. Comparisons such as ==, !=, <, and >= produce bool. Combine Boolean conditions with && (AND), || (OR), and ! (NOT). Assignment = is different from comparison ==. A u8 fits 0 through 255; choose a larger type when needed. Overflow can panic with overflow checks enabled; wrapping behavior is not promotion.

Which expression compares two values?

count = 3 count == 3 let count = 3 Check answer

docs.title: Runnable example
docs.text:
fn main() {
    let count: i32 = 5;
    let divisor: i32 = 2;
    let whole = count / divisor;
    let fraction = 5.0_f64 / 2.0;
    let enabled: bool = true;
    let initial: char = 'λ';
    assert_eq!(whole, 2);
    assert_eq!(count % divisor, 1);
    assert_eq!(fraction, 2.5);
    assert!(enabled && count > 0);
    assert_eq!(initial, 'λ');
    println!("whole: {whole}, fraction: {fraction}, initial: {initial}");
}

rustc examples/01-fundamentals/03-scalar-types-and-operators/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-fundamentals-3
/tmp/rust-fundamentals-3

Expected output:

whole: 2, fraction: 2.5, initial: λ

docs.title: Topic 4: Arrays, tuples, strings, and vectors
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to

  • Choose arrays, tuples, strings, and vectors.
  • Use indexing, methods, and tuple destructuring.
  • Distinguish byte lengths from Unicode scalar counts.

Prerequisite: Topic 3: Scalar types and operators.

docs.title: Store related values
docs.text:
An array has a fixed number of elements of one type. A tuple groups a fixed set of values that may have different types. A vector is a growable sequence of one element type.

let fixed: [i32; 3] = [2, 4, 6];
let summary: (usize, i64) = (fixed.len(), 12);
let (count, total) = summary; // Destructure a tuple.
println!("first: {}, count: {count}, total: {total}", fixed[0]);

let mut numbers: Vec<i32> = vec![3, -1, 8];
numbers.push(2);
println!("length: {}, values: {numbers:?}", numbers.len());

Indexes start at zero. fixed[3] is out of bounds for a three-element array. Indexing outside a sequence's bounds panics; numbers.get(3) instead returns an Option, representing either a present or missing element. Module 3 explains Option in detail.

let greeting: &str = "Hello"; // Borrowed text, here a string literal.
let mut title = String::from(greeting); // Owned, growable UTF-8 text.
title.push_str(", Rust");
println!("{title}");

String and Vec own their stored data; &str and &[T] provide borrowed views. For now, read &numbers as “let this function read my numbers.” Module 2 develops the ownership rules.

Text is UTF-8: "é".len() is 2 bytes, while "é".chars().count() is 1 Unicode scalar value. Rust does not allow text[0] on a string. Use .chars() when iterating over Unicode scalar values.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
Which choice fits a list of numbers that grows as values arrive?

A tuple with a fixed set of fields A fixed-length array Vec<i32> with push Check answer

Why does "é".len() return 2?

It counts UTF-8 bytes It counts two words All characters occupy two bytes Check answer

docs.title: Runnable example
docs.text:
fn main() {
    let fixed: [i32; 3] = [2, 4, 6];
    let (count, total): (usize, i64) = (fixed.len(), 12);
    assert_eq!(fixed[0], 2);
    assert_eq!((count, total), (3, 12));
    let mut numbers = vec![3, -1, 8];
    numbers.push(2);
    assert_eq!(numbers.len(), 4);
    let greeting: &str = "Hello";
    let mut title = String::from(greeting);
    title.push_str(", Rust");
    assert_eq!(title, "Hello, Rust");
    assert_eq!("é".len(), 2);
    assert_eq!("é".chars().count(), 1);
    println!("count: {count}, total: {total}, values: {numbers:?}");
    println!("{title}");
}

/tmp/rust-fundamentals-4

Hello, Rust

docs.title: Topic 5: Functions, statements, and expressions
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to

  • Define typed parameters and return values.
  • Use tail expressions and early returns.
  • Explain semicolons and the unit type.

Prerequisite: Topic 4: Arrays, tuples, strings, and vectors.

docs.title: Give behavior a name
docs.text:
Functions name reusable behavior. Parameters have types, and -> introduces the return type. An expression produces a value; a semicolon usually turns that expression into a statement whose result is discarded.

fn double(value: i32) -> i32 {
    value * 2 // The final expression returns the result.
}

fn describe(value: i32) -> &'static str {
    if value >= 0 { "nonnegative" } else { "negative" }
}

An if can itself be an expression. Both branches here return text of the same type. &'static str here refers to string literals that remain valid for the whole program; detailed lifetime syntax comes later. Use return value; when an early return makes the function clearer.

Adding a semicolon after value * 2 makes double return (), the unit type (“no meaningful result”), instead of the required i32.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
What happens if double ends with value * 2;?

Compilation fails because the function returns unit instead of i32 The function automatically returns zero Rust ignores the semicolon Check answer

What does -> i32 describe?

The number of arguments The function return type The type of every local binding Check answer

docs.title: Runnable example
docs.text:
fn double(value: i32) -> i32 {
    value * 2
}

fn nonnegative(value: i32) -> i32 {
    if value < 0 {
        return 0;
    }
    value
}

fn main() {
    assert_eq!(double(3), 6);
    assert_eq!(double(0), 0);
    assert_eq!(double(-2), -4);
    assert_eq!(nonnegative(-2), 0);
    assert_eq!(nonnegative(3), 3);
    println!("double: {}, clamped: {}", double(3), nonnegative(-2));
}

Run from the repository root:

rustc examples/01-fundamentals/05-functions-statements-expressions/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-fundamentals-5
/tmp/rust-fundamentals-5

Expected output:

double: 6, clamped: 0

docs.text:
What is a useful distinction between an expression and a statement?

Every statement returns an integer Expressions cannot appear inside functions An expression produces a value; a semicolon usually discards it Check answer

docs.title: Topic 6: Conditions and pattern basics
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to

  • Use Boolean conditions and if expressions.
  • Match simple patterns and a wildcard.
  • Explain exhaustive matches.

Prerequisite: Topic 5: Functions, statements, and expressions.

docs.title: Boolean conditions
docs.text:
if needs a Boolean condition. Use these operators to compare values and combine conditions:

  • == — equality: count == 0 checks whether count equals zero.
  • > — greater than: count > 0 checks whether count is above zero.
  • < — less than: count < 10 checks whether count is below ten.
  • && — Boolean AND: count > 0 && count < 10 requires both conditions to be true.
  • || — Boolean OR: count == 0 || count == 1 requires at least one condition to be true.
  • ! — Boolean NOT: !enabled reverses the Boolean value of enabled.

docs.title: if expressions
docs.text:
An if can produce a value:

let label = if count == 0 {
    "empty"
} else {
    "nonempty"
};

Its branches must have compatible types. Unlike some languages, Rust does not treat integers as truth values: if count is invalid.

docs.title: match patterns
docs.text:
match chooses a branch by pattern and must cover all possible inputs. In this example, the patterns 0 and 1 match those exact counts. &'static str here means a reference to a string literal valid for the whole program; detailed lifetime syntax comes later.

fn size_label(count: usize) -> &'static str {
    match count {
        0 => "empty",
        1 => "single",
        _ => "multiple", // Wildcard covers every remaining value.
    }
}

Read the symbols in this function as follows:

  • -> — return-type marker: -> &'static str declares the function's return type.
  • => — match-arm separator: 0 => "empty" connects a pattern to the expression evaluated when it matches.
  • _ — wildcard pattern: _ => "multiple" handles any count not matched by an earlier arm.

docs.title: Wildcards and exhaustive matches
docs.text: The _ wildcard pattern matches any value not handled by an earlier arm. It covers counts 2 and above here, making the match exhaustive: every possible input has a branch. Without it, the compiler rejects this match because 0 and 1 alone do not cover every usize value.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
What does the wildcard _ do in size_label?

It ignores the entire match It handles all values not matched by earlier arms It means only zero Check answer

Which condition is valid when count is an integer?

if count if count > 0 if "yes" Check answer

docs.title: Runnable example
docs.text:
fn size_label(count: usize) -> &'static str {
    match count {
        0 => "empty",
        1 => "single",
        _ => "multiple",
    }
}

fn main() {
    let count = 3;
    let label = if count == 0 { "empty" } else { "nonempty" };
    assert_eq!(label, "nonempty");
    assert_eq!(size_label(0), "empty");
    assert_eq!(size_label(1), "single");
    assert_eq!(size_label(3), "multiple");
    println!("if: {label}, match: {}", size_label(count));
}

Run from the repository root:

rustc examples/01-fundamentals/06-conditions-and-patterns/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-fundamentals-6
/tmp/rust-fundamentals-6

Expected output:

if: nonempty, match: multiple

docs.text:
Why must match cover every possible input?

Every input needs a defined branch It must always clone the input It can only accept Boolean inputs Check answer

docs.title: Topic 7: Loops and ranges
docs.text:
By the end, you will be able to

  • Use exclusive and inclusive ranges and reverse iteration.
    • Choose a step size with step_by().
    • Count backward with rev().
  • Choose for, while, and loop.
  • Control repetition with break and continue.

Prerequisite: Topic 6: Conditions and pattern basics.

docs.title: Repeat a step
docs.text: Use for to visit items or a range, while to repeat while a condition holds, and loop to repeat until an explicit break.

docs.title: Ranges: choose the values to visit
docs.text:
A range describes a sequence of values using a start and an end. In integer loops, values advance by one. The punctuation determines whether the end is included; the start is included in both forms below.

Range Values visited Meaning 1..4 1, 2, 3 Excludes the end, 4 1..=4 1, 2, 3, 4 Includes the end, 4 0..3 0, 1, 2 Three values starting at zero 3..3 None An exclusive range with equal bounds is empty 3..=3 3 An inclusive range with equal bounds visits once

Use an exclusive range for zero-based positions: a collection of length 3 has indices 0..3. Use an inclusive range when the final value itself belongs in the calculation, such as summing 1 through 5.

Writing the larger number first does not make a countdown: 4..1 is empty. To visit the same values backward, reverse an ascending range with .rev(). These examples use integer ranges; ranges do not automatically interpret floating-point bounds as a series of fractional steps.

More iterator methods later in the course

Ranges support iterator methods beyond rev() and step_by(). Module 2, Topic 6 introduces sum(), map(), and collect() through collection iterators. Module 8: Closures and advanced iterators will cover these in depth, plus filter(), take(), skip(), enumerate(), and count(). Module 8 is planned; for now, focus on ranges, stepping, and the three loop forms below.

docs.title: Choose a step size
docs.text:
Use .step_by(2) to visit every second value instead of every value:

for number in (0..=10).step_by(2) {
    println!("{number}"); // 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, each on its own line
}

For a countdown, reverse the range before stepping:

for number in (0..=10).rev().step_by(2) {
    println!("{number}"); // 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, each on its own line
}

The step is a positive usize: .step_by(0) panics. Use .rev() for backward iteration rather than a negative step. The first value is visited, then the iterator skips values according to the step; the end is reached only if it falls on a step. For example, (0..=5).step_by(2) visits 0, 2, 4.

docs.title: Count in reverse
docs.text:
Countdown: count backward with .rev()

Use .rev() on an ascending range to count backward. (1..=3).rev() visits 3, 2, 1, including both endpoints.

for number in (1..=3).rev() {
    println!("{number}");
}

Output:

3
2
1

The parentheses group the range before calling .rev(). Compare (1..4).rev(): because 4 is excluded, it visits 3, 2, 1. Reversing an empty range still visits nothing. The complete runnable example below also checks the countdown order with an assertion.

docs.title: for: visit each value
docs.text:
Use for when you want to visit each value in a range or collection. The range 1..=3 includes 3; 1..3 stops before 3.

let mut total = 0;
for number in 1..=3 {
    total += number;
}
println!("{total}"); // 6

Which values does 1..3 visit?

1, 2, 3 1, 2 0, 1, 2 Check answer

docs.title: while: repeat while a condition is true
docs.text:
while checks its condition before each pass. This countdown runs twice; starting at zero would skip the body entirely.

let mut remaining = 2;
while remaining > 0 {
    remaining -= 1;
}
println!("{remaining}"); // 0

Ensure the condition can change, or the loop may never finish.

docs.title: loop: repeat until break
docs.text:
loop repeats without a condition at the top. Use break to exit it. Here, break attempts also supplies the value assigned to finished.

let mut attempts = 0;
let finished = loop {
    attempts += 1;
    if attempts == 2 {
        break attempts; // A loop can return a value.
    }
};
println!("{finished}"); // 2

docs.title: break and continue
docs.text: continue skips to the next iteration; break exits the loop. The snippets above belong inside main; the complete runnable program follows.

docs.title: Runnable example
docs.text:
fn main() {
    let mut total = 0;
    for number in 1..=3 {
        total += number;
    }
    assert_eq!(total, 6);
    let mut remaining = 2;
    while remaining > 0 {
        remaining -= 1;
    }
    assert_eq!(remaining, 0);
    let mut attempts = 0;
    let finished = loop {
        attempts += 1;
        if attempts == 2 {
            break attempts;
        }
    };
    assert_eq!(finished, 2);
    let mut odd_total = 0;
    for number in 1..=4 {
        if number % 2 == 0 {
            continue;
        }
        odd_total += number;
    }
    assert_eq!(odd_total, 4);
    println!("sum: {total}, remaining: {remaining}, finished: {finished}, odd sum: {odd_total}");
    let mut countdown = Vec::new();
    for number in (1..=4).rev() {
        countdown.push(number);
        println!("{number}");
    }
    assert_eq!(countdown, [4, 3, 2, 1]);
}

4
3
2

docs.title: Focus on continue
docs.text:
Here is just the odd-number loop from the example. % gives the remainder, so number % 2 == 0 checks whether the number is even.

let mut odd_total = 0;
for number in 1..=4 {
    if number % 2 == 0 {
        continue;
    }
    odd_total += number;
}

When number is 2, what does continue do?

Stops the loop, so 3 and 4 are never visited Adds 2 to odd_total, then moves on to 3 Skips odd_total += number for 2, then starts the next pass with number equal to 3 Check answer

docs.title: 1. Sum an inclusive range
docs.text:
Sum 1 through 5 and assert that the result is 15.

Solution: sum 1 through 5 
fn main() {
    let mut total = 0;
    for number in 1..=5 {
        total += number;
    }
    assert_eq!(total, 15);
    println!("total: {total}");

docs.title: 2. Sum only odd numbers
docs.text:
Sum only the odd numbers from 1 through 5 and assert that the result is 9. Use continue to skip even numbers.

Solution: skip even numbers 
fn main() {
    let mut total = 0;
    for number in 1..=5 {
        if number % 2 == 0 {
            continue;
        }
        total += number;
    }
    assert_eq!(total, 9);
    println!("odd total: {total}");
}

For 2 and 4, continue skips the addition. Only 1 + 3 + 5 contributes to the sum. Expected output: odd total: 9.

docs.title: 3. Iterate over an empty range
docs.text:
Try an empty range such as 3..3 and check that the accumulator stays zero.

Solution: an empty range adds nothing 
fn main() {
    let mut total = 0;
    for number in 3..3 {
        total += number;
    }
    assert_eq!(total, 0);
    println!("empty-range total: {total}");
}

3..3 starts at 3 but excludes its end, also 3. There are no values to visit, so the body never runs. Expected output: empty-range total: 0.

docs.title: 4. Start the countdown at zero
docs.text:
Change the countdown start to 0 and confirm the loop runs zero times. Count loop iterations to verify this directly.

Solution: check the condition before the first pass 
fn main() {
    let mut remaining = 0;
    let mut iterations = 0;
    while remaining > 0 {
        iterations += 1;
        remaining -= 1;
    }
    assert_eq!(remaining, 0);
    assert_eq!(iterations, 0);
    println!("remaining: {remaining}, iterations: {iterations}");
}

while checks remaining > 0 before entering the body. It is false immediately, so neither the counter nor remaining changes. Expected output: remaining: 0, iterations: 0.

docs.title: Cargo project and complete demo
docs.text:
The demo uses this layout:

number-summary/
├── Cargo.toml       # Package name, version, and Rust edition.
└── src/
    └── main.rs      # Entry point, helper functions, and unit tests.

Cargo generates Cargo.lock to record dependency resolution and target/ for build output. No third-party dependencies are required here.

The program collects numbers, borrows them to calculate a count and sum, destructures the returned tuple, and prints the result.

flowchart LR
    A[Create numbers] --> B[Pass a borrowed slice]
    B --> C[Loop and accumulate total]
    C --> D[Return count and total tuple]
    D --> E[Print summary]
fn summarize(values: &[i32]) -> (usize, i64) {
    // A slice lets us read either an array or a vector without consuming it.
    let mut total: i64 = 0;
    for &value in values {
        // Widen each i32 before adding; keep the demo inputs small.
        total += i64::from(value);
    }
    (values.len(), total) // No semicolon: this tuple is the returned value.
}

fn size_label(count: usize) -> &'static str {
    match count {
        0 => "empty",
        1 => "single",
        _ => "multiple",
    }
}

fn main() {
    let fixed = [2, 4, 6];
    let mut numbers = vec![3, -1, 8];
    numbers.push(2); // Vec can grow; arrays have a fixed length.

    let mut title = String::from("Number");
    title.push_str(" summary");
    println!("{title}");

    let (count, total) = summarize(&numbers);
    println!("count: {count}, total: {total}");
    println!("size: {}", size_label(count));
    println!("positive total: {}", total > 0);

    let (array_count, array_total) = summarize(&fixed);
    println!("array count: {array_count}, total: {array_total}");

    let mut remaining = 2;
    while remaining > 0 {
        println!("countdown: {remaining}");
        remaining -= 1;
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn summarizes_mixed_values() {
        assert_eq!(summarize(&[3, -1, 8, 2]), (4, 12));
    }

    #[test]
    fn summarizes_empty_input() {
        assert_eq!(summarize(&[]), (0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn summarizes_negative_values() {
        assert_eq!(summarize(&[-3, -2]), (2, -5));
    }

    #[test]
    fn widens_before_addition() {
        assert_eq!(summarize(&[i32::MAX, i32::MAX]), (2, 4_294_967_294));
    }

    #[test]
    fn classifies_sizes() {
        assert_eq!(size_label(0), "empty");
        assert_eq!(size_label(1), "single");
        assert_eq!(size_label(3), "multiple");
    }
}

Why does the demo use an i64 accumulator?

To make every possible input overflow-proof To widen i32 values before adding the small sample inputs To turn numbers into text Check answer

The for &value in values pattern copies each small integer out of its shared reference; it does not consume the caller's collection. The accumulator uses i64, so addition of the sample i32 values fits comfortably. This is a small-input teaching example, not an arbitrary-size numeric aggregation API.

positive total: true

docs.title: Values and variables
docs.text:
A value is data such as 42 or the text stored in a String. A variable is a name that lets the program use a value:

let score = 42;

Here, 42 is the value and score is the variable that owns it. By default, variables are immutable, so use let mut when the binding itself must change:

let mut score = 42;
score = 43;

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Scope is the part of the program where a variable is valid. A variable starts when its let statement runs and ends at the closing brace of its block.

fn main() {
    let outside = "available here";

    {
        let inside = "available only in this block";
        println!("{outside}, {inside}");
    }

    println!("{outside}");
    // println!("{inside}"); // would fail: `inside` is out of scope
}

Rust drops a value when its owner leaves scope. For a small stack value, this usually means the storage is no longer needed. For a heap-backed value such as String or Vec<T>, Rust also releases the heap allocation automatically.

flowchart TD
  A[Enter block] --> B[Create owner and value]
  B --> C[Use value]
  C --> D[Leave block]
  D --> E[Drop value]
  E --> F[Release owned resources]

docs.title: Stack and heap, briefly
docs.text:
The stack is fast storage for values with a known, simple layout, such as integers. The heap stores data whose size can change or whose ownership must outlive a single expression. A String value keeps a small handle on the stack and its text in a heap allocation.

The important ownership lesson is that the variable still owns the complete String, including the heap data. When the variable leaves scope, Rust cleans up the allocation without a manual free call.

The same rule applies to Vec<T>. A vector stores its elements in a heap allocation, while the Vec handle on the stack tracks the allocation. The variable owns both the handle and the elements it contains:

{
    let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];
    numbers.push(4);
    println!("numbers: {numbers:?}");
} // numbers and its heap allocation are dropped here

Expected output:

numbers: [1, 2, 3, 4]

The vector is automatically cleaned up when the block ends. No manual deallocation is needed.

docs.title: Why heap-backed types matter
docs.text:
Real programs often need data whose size is known only while the program is running: user input, a file, a network response, or a collection of records. String, Vec<T>, and similar types keep that changing data on the heap while their small ownership handle stays on the stack.

That extra allocation is useful because the data can grow, but it also creates resources that must have one clear owner. Rust's ownership rules make sure the allocation is released exactly once and cannot be used after its owner has gone away. Borrowing then lets another function temporarily read or modify the data without taking ownership:

fn add_label(labels: &mut Vec<String>) {
    labels.push(String::from("Rust"));
}

fn main() {
    let mut labels = vec![String::from("safe")];
    add_label(&mut labels); // borrowed temporarily, then returned to `labels`
    println!("{labels:?}");
} // `labels` owns the vector and its strings until cleanup

Expected output:

["safe", "Rust"]

This is why heap-backed types are central to ownership and borrowing: they let Rust support flexible, useful data structures without requiring manual free, while still making the lifetime and access rules explicit.

docs.title: Memory after each step
docs.text: The diagrams below are conceptual. They explain ownership and lifetime, not literal addresses, stack offsets, allocator metadata, or an exact compiler layout.

docs.title: Step 1: create score
docs.text:
let score = 42;
Area State Stack score owns the integer value 42. Heap No allocation is needed for this integer. Scope score is valid until the end of main.

docs.title: Step 2: create message
docs.text:
let message = String::from("Rust owns its data");
Area State Stack message owns a String handle containing a pointer, length, and capacity. Heap The string characters are stored in an allocation owned by message. Scope message is valid until the end of main.

docs.title: Step 3: enter the inner scope
docs.text:
{
    let temporary = String::from("temporary value");
}
Area State Stack score, message, and temporary are valid in the inner block. Heap There are separate allocations for message and temporary. Scope temporary is valid only inside the inner block.

docs.title: Step 4: leave the inner scope
docs.text:
When the closing brace runs, temporary leaves scope first:

Area State Stack The temporary binding is gone. score and message remain. Heap The allocation owned by temporary is released. message remains allocated. Scope Code after the block can still use score and message.

docs.title: Step 5: leave main
docs.text:
At the end of main, Rust drops the remaining owners automatically:

Area State Stack score and the message handle leave scope. Heap The allocation owned by message is released. Result No manual free call is needed.

docs.title: The intuition: one owner, one cleanup
docs.text:
For a heap-backed value such as String, the variable contains a small handle that points to data on the heap. If Rust copied that handle during assignment, two variables could try to release the same allocation. Rust avoids that problem by moving ownership: the destination becomes the owner and the source binding is no longer usable.

let first = String::from("hello");
let second = first; // ownership moves from `first` to `second`
println!("{second}");

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
What happens to first after let second = first when the value is a String?

It owns a second copy of the heap text It is moved from and cannot be used It becomes a shared global variable Check answer

The text is not copied by this assignment. The String handle and its heap allocation now belong to second. The compiler rejects this because first is no longer an owner:

// println!("{first}");

This is a compile-time rule, so the program cannot accidentally use a moved value or free its allocation twice.

The diagram is conceptual: it shows ownership and pointers, not literal addresses or the exact allocator representation.

docs.title: Compiler errors are ownership feedback
docs.text:
When the compiler reports borrow of moved value, read it as a short ownership history. It means:

  1. A value had an owner.
  2. An operation moved ownership somewhere else.
  3. Later code tried to use the old binding.

Here is a deliberately tricky example. The println! looks harmless because it only reads title, but reading still requires the binding to be valid:

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Rust ownership");
    let archived_title = title; // The String moves to `archived_title`.

    println!("archived: {archived_title}");
    println!("current: {title}"); // Error: `title` was moved above.
}

The compiler rejects the whole program before it runs. This matters because a use-after-free would otherwise be a runtime memory-safety bug: the old binding could point at storage that another owner already released. Rejecting the code at compile time means every execution of the compiled program follows a valid ownership path, without adding a runtime ownership counter for ordinary String values.

The diagnostic usually points to both sides of the story:

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `title`
  --> src/main.rs:6:29
   |
3  |     let archived_title = title;
   |                          ----- value moved here
...
6  |     println!("current: {title}");
   |                          ^^^^^ value borrowed here after move

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
What does borrow of moved value: title tell you?

The compiler detected a slow heap allocation while the program was running title was copied twice and needs manual cleanup title was moved earlier, then used again later Check answer

The fix is to choose the intended ownership design. Use the new owner:

println!("current: {archived_title}");

Or make an explicit independent copy when both values must own their data:

let archived_title = title.clone();
println!("current: {title}");
println!("archived: {archived_title}");

clone() is an explicit heap-data copy, so it has a cost and communicates a different design from a cheap move of the String handle.

docs.title: Moving into and out of functions
docs.text:
Passing an owned value to a function uses the same rule. The function becomes the owner for the duration of the call, then drops the value when its parameter leaves scope:

fn take_ownership(text: String) {
    println!("inside function: {text}");
} // `text` is dropped here

let message = String::from("hello");
take_ownership(message);
// `message` cannot be used here because ownership moved into the function.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
What does take_ownership(message) do?

It always clones message It only borrows message It moves ownership into the function Check answer

If the caller needs the value afterward, the function can return ownership:

fn give_back(text: String) -> String {
    text
}

let message = give_back(String::from("hello"));
println!("{message}");

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
Why can the caller use the result of give_back?

The function returns ownership to the caller Rust makes every function parameter global The heap allocation is never cleaned up Check answer

Returning ownership works, but borrowing is often a better fit when a function only needs temporary access. The next lessons build on this distinction.

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
The lesson displays the same source file used by the matching demo:

fn take_ownership(text: String) {
    // `text` is the owner inside this function.
    println!("inside function: {text}");
} // `text` leaves scope, so Rust drops the String here.

fn give_back(text: String) -> String {
    // The function receives ownership and returns it to its caller.
    text
}

fn main() {
    let first = String::from("hello");
    let second = first; // Move the String handle and heap allocation to `second`.

    // `first` cannot be used here: it no longer owns the String.
    println!("after move: {second}");

    take_ownership(second); // Move ownership into the function.

    let returned = give_back(String::from("ownership returned"));
    println!("returned: {returned}");
}

inside function: hello
returned: ownership returned

To make the old variable global To keep one owner responsible for cleanup To prevent all heap allocation Check answer

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Explain why simple values such as integers can be copied automatically.
  • Distinguish an implicit Copy from an explicit clone().
  • Recognize that cloning heap-backed data can allocate and copy data.
  • Use #[derive(Clone)] when a type has a meaningful duplication operation.

docs.title: Copy: small values can have two bindings
docs.text:
Some types have a simple, fixed-size representation and no resource that needs special cleanup. These types can implement Copy. Assignment copies the value, so both bindings remain valid:

let attempts = 3_u8;
let backup_attempts = attempts; // The number is copied.

println!("{attempts}");
println!("{backup_attempts}");

The compiler knows that copying a u8 does not create two owners of the same heap allocation. Common Copy types include integers, floating-point values, booleans, characters, and tuples made only from Copy types.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
Why can the code use both attempts and backup_attempts?

u8 implements Copy Rust stores every integer on the heap The first variable was automatically cloned with a heap allocation Check answer

docs.title: Clone: an explicit duplicate
docs.text:
String does not implement Copy because copying its handle would duplicate the ownership of one heap allocation. It does implement Clone, which makes a separate copy when you ask for one:

let original = String::from("primary");
let duplicate = original.clone(); // Explicitly copy the heap text.

println!("original: {original}");
println!("duplicate: {duplicate}");

After clone(), each String owns a different heap allocation. The operation can be more expensive than a move because it copies the characters and may allocate memory. That explicit cost is useful: the code shows that two owners are intentional.

The diagram is conceptual. It shows ownership relationships, not literal addresses or the exact internal representation of a Rust value.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
What does original.clone() provide for a String?

A second binding to the same allocation without another owner rule A separate owned copy of the string data A shared reference that lives forever Check answer

docs.title: Clone for structs
docs.text:
A type can derive Clone when each of its fields can be cloned. The generated implementation clones each field, so the String field gets its own heap copy:

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
struct Settings {
    retries: u8,
    label: String,
}

let settings = Settings {
    retries: 3,
    label: String::from("demo"),
};
let settings_copy = settings.clone();

The u8 field is cheap to copy, while the String field performs a heap-data clone. Deriving Clone is convenient, but it should still match the meaning of duplicating the type in the program.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
What happens when settings.clone() is called?

The original settings value is destroyed Only the retries field is copied A new Settings value is created with cloned fields Check answer

docs.title: Choose the operation that expresses intent
docs.text: Use a move when one owner should continue with the value. Use Copy when a small value naturally has independent duplicates. Use clone() when two owners need independent heap-backed data and the copy cost is acceptable. If a function only needs temporary access, borrowing is often better than either a move or a clone.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
Why is clone() explicit for a heap-backed type?

Rust cannot move heap-backed values It may allocate and copy data, so the cost should be visible It prevents the original value from being dropped Check answer

docs.text:

    retries: u8,
    label: String,
}

fn main() {
    let attempts = 3;
    let backup_attempts = attempts; // `u8` is Copy, so both bindings stay usable.
    println!("attempts: {attempts}, backup: {backup_attempts}");

    let original = String::from("primary");
    let duplicate = original.clone(); // Explicitly copy the heap text.
    println!("original: {original}, duplicate: {duplicate}");

    let settings = Settings {
        retries: attempts,
        label: String::from("demo"),
    };
    let settings_copy = settings.clone(); // Derive Clone deep-copies its fields.
    println!("settings: {settings:?}");
    println!("settings copy: {settings_copy:?}");
    println!("fields: retries={}, label={}", settings.retries, settings.label);
}

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Create a mutable reference with &mut T.
  • Change an owner's value through a mutable reference.
  • Explain why Rust allows only one active mutable reference.
  • Recognize conflicts between shared and mutable references.
