docs.title: Exclusive access without moving ownership
docs.text:
A shared reference &T can read a value. A mutable reference &mut T can read and change it, but it gives one borrower exclusive access for its lifetime. The owner is temporarily lending control, not giving ownership away:

fn add_one(value: &mut i32) {
    *value += 1; // Dereference, then update the owner's integer.
}

let mut score = 41;
add_one(&mut score);
println!("{score}"); // The owner uses the value after the borrow ends.

The binding must be declared mut because the value is being changed. The function parameter is &mut i32 because the function needs exclusive access to the caller's integer.

The diagram is conceptual. The mutable reference is shown as temporary exclusive access to the same storage, not as a second allocation or owner.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
What does &mut score provide to add_one?

A new owner that will drop the integer Temporary exclusive access to change the owner's integer A read-only copy of the integer Check answer

docs.title: Mutable borrowing with heap-backed data
docs.text:
The same rule works for String, Vec<T>, and other owned values. A function can modify the allocation through &mut without taking ownership:

fn add_suffix(text: &mut String) {
    text.push_str("!");
}

let mut message = String::from("Rust");
add_suffix(&mut message);
println!("{message}");

message still owns the String and its heap allocation. The function only gets a temporary exclusive view, so cleanup remains the owner's responsibility.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
After add_suffix(&mut message) returns, who owns the String?

add_suffix forever owns it The mutable reference becomes a second owner message remains the owner Check answer

docs.title: Why only one mutable reference?
docs.text:
If two mutable references could exist at once, both could write the same value without coordination. Rust prevents that data race even in single-threaded code:

let mut score = 10;
let first = &mut score;
// let second = &mut score; // Error: cannot borrow `score` as mutable twice.
*first += 1;

One mutable reference has exclusive access. Once first is no longer used, a new mutable borrow can begin:

let mut score = 10;
{
    let first = &mut score;
    *first += 1;
}
let second = &mut score;
*second += 1;
println!("{score}");

Rust uses the last use of a reference when it can prove that a borrow has ended, so the scopes can often be shorter than the surrounding block.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
Why does Rust reject two active &mut references to the same value?

To prevent conflicting writes through two exclusive access paths Because mutable references always allocate a second value Because only integers can be borrowed Check answer

docs.title: Shared and mutable borrows cannot overlap
docs.text:
A shared reference promises that the value will only be read. A mutable reference promises exclusive access. Those promises conflict, so Rust rejects this pattern:

let mut message = String::from("Rust");
let view = &message;
// let edit = &mut message; // Error: shared and mutable borrows overlap.
println!("{view}");

End the shared borrow before requesting mutation:

let mut message = String::from("Rust");
{
    let view = &message;
    println!("before: {view}");
}
let edit = &mut message;
edit.push('!');
println!("after: {message}");

This rule prevents a reader from observing a value while another access path is changing it.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
Why can &message and &mut message not overlap?

Shared references always move the String A reader and an exclusive writer would have conflicting access Mutable references can only point to stack integers Check answer

docs.title: Reborrowing: a short borrow of a mutable borrow
docs.text:
While holding &mut T, you can create a shorter temporary borrow for a call. The original mutable access becomes usable again after that shorter borrow ends:

fn show(value: &i32) {
    println!("current: {value}");
}

fn update(value: &mut i32) {
    show(&*value); // Short shared reborrow for this call.
    *value += 1;   // The mutable borrow is usable again.
}

The &*value expression temporarily views the value through a shared reference. It does not create another owner, and it does not make the mutable borrow permanent.

    // Dereference the mutable reference to change the owner's value.

}

    // The function mutates the caller's String without taking ownership.
    text.push_str("!");
}

fn main() {
    let mut score = 41;
    add_one(&mut score); // Temporarily lend exclusive access.
    println!("score: {score}"); // The borrow ended when the call finished.

    let mut message = String::from("Rust");
    add_suffix(&mut message);
    println!("message: {message}");
}

docs.title: A brief reminder about Rust collections
docs.text:
Collections hold a variable number of values. Common examples are:

  • Vec<T>: an ordered, growable sequence.
  • String: growable UTF-8 text.
  • HashMap<K, V>: key-value associations.

These collections usually keep a small handle on the stack and their elements in a heap allocation. The collection owns that allocation and its elements, so Rust needs to know whether an operation is borrowing the elements, changing them, or consuming the collection.

let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];
numbers.push(4); // The Vec owns its elements and may grow its allocation.

Borrowing lets a function work with the elements while the collection remains owned by its caller.

The diagram is conceptual. It shows the Vec handle, heap elements, and iterator access paths, not literal addresses or allocator metadata.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
What does a Vec<T> own?

Only the variable name, never its elements Its collection handle, heap allocation, and elements A global copy shared by all vectors Check answer

docs.title: iter: read elements without consuming the collection
docs.text:
Calling iter() creates an iterator that borrows each element as &T. The collection remains available after the loop:

fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    values.iter().sum()
}

let numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];
let total = sum_values(&numbers);
println!("total: {total}");
println!("still owned: {numbers:?}");

The function accepts a slice, a borrowed view of the vector's elements. It does not move the Vec and it does not clone the values.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
What does numbers.iter() yield?

Shared references to the elements Owned elements after deleting the Vec Mutable references that can always resize the Vec Check answer

docs.title: iter_mut: change elements in place
docs.text:
When the collection is mutable, iter_mut() yields &mut T one element at a time:

fn add_one_to_each(values: &mut [i32]) {
    for value in values.iter_mut() {
        *value += 1;
    }
}

let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];
add_one_to_each(&mut numbers);
println!("{numbers:?}"); // [2, 3, 4]

The iterator provides one mutable element borrow at a time. It does not give the loop unlimited mutable aliases to the same element.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
What is the purpose of iter_mut()?

To consume the Vec and return owned elements To create a cloned Vec automatically To mutate elements through temporary mutable references Check answer

docs.title: into_iter: consume and own the elements
docs.text:
into_iter() on an owned Vec<T> consumes the vector and yields owned T values. After the call, the original vector cannot be used:

let numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];
let doubled: Vec<i32> = numbers
    .into_iter()
    .map(|value| value * 2)
    .collect();

println!("{doubled:?}");
// println!("{numbers:?}"); // Error: numbers was consumed.

This is useful when ownership should move into a new collection or processing pipeline. It avoids cloning each element, but the source collection is no longer available.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
What happens when numbers.into_iter() is called on an owned Vec?

The Vec is borrowed and remains usable forever The Vec is consumed and its elements are yielded by value Every element is cloned before iteration Check answer

docs.title: Do not mutate while an element is borrowed
docs.text:
A vector may move its heap allocation when it grows. Therefore Rust rejects a mutation that could invalidate an element reference:

let mut words = vec![String::from("Rust")];
let first = &words[0];
// words.push(String::from("safe")); // Error: cannot mutably borrow `words`.
println!("{first}");

End the element borrow before changing the vector:

let mut words = vec![String::from("Rust")];
{
    let first = &words[0];
    println!("before: {first}");
}
words.push(String::from("safe"));
println!("after: {words:?}");

The compiler protects both ownership and reference validity: no reference may continue pointing into a collection whose storage has been invalidated.

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
The lesson displays the same source file used by the matching demo:

fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    // `iter` borrows each element, so the caller keeps the Vec.
    values.iter().sum()
}

fn add_one_to_each(values: &mut [i32]) {
    // `iter_mut` gives one mutable borrow of each element in turn.
    for value in values.iter_mut() {
        *value += 1;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3];

    let total = sum_values(&numbers);
    println!("total: {total}");

    add_one_to_each(&mut numbers);
    println!("updated: {numbers:?}");

    // `into_iter` consumes the Vec and yields owned elements.
    let owned_values: Vec<i32> = numbers.into_iter().map(|value| value * 2).collect();
    println!("consumed into new Vec: {owned_values:?}");
}

  -o /tmp/rust-collection-borrows
/tmp/rust-collection-borrows

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Explain a slice as a borrowed view of part or all of a collection.
  • Use &str for read-only text APIs.
  • Use &[T] for functions that read sequences of values.
  • Return a slice tied to an input instead of returning a dangling reference.

docs.title: What is a slice?
docs.text:
A slice is a borrowed view into existing data. It does not own the data and it does not copy the elements. Conceptually, a slice contains a pointer to the first item and a length:

let numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40];
let middle: &[i32] = &numbers[1..3];

println!("{middle:?}"); // [20, 30]

The range 1..3 includes index 1 and stops before index 3. The original array owns all four values; middle only views the two selected values.

The diagram is conceptual. A slice is shown as a pointer and length, not as a second allocation or an owner.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
What does a slice contain conceptually?

A new owned copy of every selected element A pointer and length describing a borrowed range Only the allocation capacity of a collection Check answer

docs.title: &str: a text API boundary
docs.text:
String owns growable UTF-8 text. &str is a borrowed view of UTF-8 text. A read-only function should usually accept &str instead of &String because both a String and a string literal can provide a &str:

fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    text.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")
}

let owned = String::from("Rust makes views useful");
let literal = "Rust is fast";

println!("{}", first_word(&owned));
println!("{}", first_word(literal));

The returned &str points into the input. It is valid only while the input text remains valid, so the function cannot outlive or out-own its argument.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
Why is &str usually preferable to &String for read-only text?

It always creates a new String It transfers ownership of the caller's text It accepts text views from String values and literals Check answer

docs.title: &[T]: a sequence API boundary
docs.text:
The same idea applies to collections. A function that only reads values should usually accept &[T], not &Vec<T>:

fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    values.iter().sum()
}

let array = [1, 2, 3, 4];
let vector = vec![5, 6, 7];

println!("{}", sum_values(&array));
println!("{}", sum_values(&vector));
println!("{}", sum_values(&array[1..3]));

One signature accepts an array, a Vec, or a sub-slice. The caller keeps ownership, and the function does not need to know how the sequence was stored.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
What can a function accepting &[i32] read?

An array, a Vec, or a sub-slice of either Only a Vec with exactly one capacity Only an owned array copied into the function Check answer

docs.title: Returning a slice safely
docs.text:
A function may return a slice when the slice comes from an input that stays alive. This is a common zero-allocation pattern:

fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    text.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")
}

let sentence = String::from("borrowed result");
let word = first_word(&sentence);
println!("{word}");

The result is tied to sentence. Rust rejects a function that creates a local String and returns a reference to it because the local would be dropped on function return. If the function creates new data, return an owned String instead.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
When is returning a &str safe?

When it points to a local String created inside the function When it points into input data that remains alive Only when the text is cloned first Check answer

docs.title: AsRef: accept several view providers
docs.text:
Sometimes an API should accept several types that can cheaply provide the same borrowed view. AsRef<str> is useful for a small helper like this:

fn print_text<T: AsRef<str>>(text: T) {
    println!("{}", text.as_ref());
}

print_text("a literal");
print_text(String::from("owned text"));

The generic parameter owns its input for the duration of the call, but the function immediately borrows a &str view from it. Do not add a generic bound just to make an API look flexible: use &str when that is all the function needs. Borrow and more advanced generic bounds are useful when a collection or lookup API needs stronger equivalence guarantees.

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
The lesson displays the same source file used by the matching demo:

fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    // Return a view into the caller's text without allocating or taking ownership.
    text.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")
}

fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    // A slice accepts a Vec, an array, or part of either collection.
    values.iter().sum()
}

fn print_text<T: AsRef<str>>(text: T) {
    // AsRef lets this read from several string-like input types.
    println!("text: {}", text.as_ref());
}

fn main() {
    let sentence = String::from("Rust makes views useful");
    let first = first_word(&sentence);
    println!("first word: {first}");

    let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
    println!("array sum: {}", sum_values(&numbers));
    println!("middle sum: {}", sum_values(&numbers[1..3]));

    let owned_numbers = vec![5, 6, 7];
    println!("Vec sum: {}", sum_values(&owned_numbers));

    print_text("a literal");
    print_text(sentence.as_str());
}

docs.text:
• Trace owners and drops through nested scopes.
  • Repair a move error and explain the ownership transfer.
  • Choose copying, moving, or cloning for a stated requirement.
  • Complete and run a small program without relying on answer choices.
  • Read and update a sub-slice through borrowed iteration.
  • Return a borrowed word without cloning its text.
  • Combine borrowed processing with a final ownership-consuming step.

Prerequisites: Values and scope, Moves, Copy and Clone, Shared borrowing, Mutable borrowing, Collections and iterators, and Slices. This final module topic practices selected skills from Topics 2.1–2.7. Lifetime annotations are outside this practice set. Attempt each task before consulting the solution. docs.title: 1. Explain the terms in your own words
docs.text:
Learn this in Topic 1: Values and scope, Topic 2: Moves, and Topic 3: Copy and Clone.

For each term, give a definition and point to a concrete line in one of the exercises: value, binding, owner, scope, drop, stack, heap, move, Copy, Clone. Explain why a String binding leaving scope does not always drop its original string data: ownership may already have moved elsewhere.

Reminder: bindings and data

A String owns heap-backed text. Moving it transfers ownership without duplicating that text. Scope determines when a remaining owner is dropped.

docs.title: 2. Trace ownership before compiling
docs.text:
Learn this in Topic 1: Values and scope, Topic 2: Moves, and Topic 3: Copy and Clone.

fn main() {
    let count = 3_u32;
    let other_count = count;
    let first = String::from("Read");
    {
        let second = first;
        let third = second.clone();
        println!("{second} {third} {count} {other_count}");
    }
}

Write a table with one row after each let: usable bindings, current owners, and whether an independent heap allocation was created. Then predict which owned strings are dropped at the inner closing brace. Compile to check your predicted output, and explain why output alone cannot prove your ownership table.

Solution: trace ownership

Each row describes the state immediately after that let. Here, A and B label two independent heap allocations holding the text Read.

After statement Usable bindings String owners New independent heap allocation? let count = 3_u32; count None No, u32 needs no heap allocation let other_count = count; count, other_count None No, the integer is copied let first = String::from("Read"); count, other_count, first first owns A Yes, A let second = first; count, other_count, second second owns A No, ownership moves from first let third = second.clone(); count, other_count, second, third second owns A, third owns B Yes, B contains a copy of A's text

first is unusable after the move into second. The two integers remain usable because u32 implements Copy.

At the inner closing brace, third is dropped first, then second, in reverse declaration order. Their drops release B and A respectively. Afterward, only count and other_count remain usable. At the outer closing brace, first does not drop A again because it has been moved from.

Expected output:

Read Read 3 3

Output confirms the printed values, but it does not show which binding owns an allocation or when that allocation is released. Independent strings can print identical text. The ownership table follows from Rust's move, Copy, Clone, and scope rules.

docs.title: 3. Diagnose and repair a move
docs.text:
Learn this in Topic 2: Moves, with Topic 5: Mutable borrowing for the alternative solution.

fn decorate(mut title: String) -> String {
    title.push('!');
    title
}

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Read");
    let updated = decorate(title);
    println!("{title}");
}

Save this in a temporary Rust file and compile it. Identify the move site and the invalid later use. Repair it without cloning: keep the returned value and print Read!. Explain who owns the string inside decorate and after its return. Do not replace the function with a borrowed API for this exercise.

Solution: repair the move

decorate(title) moves the string from main into the function's title parameter. The later println!("{title}") tries to use the moved binding, so the compiler reports E0382: borrow of moved value.

Print updated, which owns the returned string:

fn decorate(mut title: String) -> String {
    title.push('!');
    title
}

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Read");
    let updated = decorate(title);
    println!("{updated}");
}

Expected output:

Read!

Inside decorate, its title parameter owns the string. mut allows the function to append !. The final expression title moves ownership back to the caller, where updated becomes the owner. The string is dropped when updated leaves scope at the end of main.

No clone is needed because the exercise requires only the updated string, with no independent copy of the original.

Alternative solution: mutable borrowing

This version explores a borrowed API. Use the first solution to complete Exercise 3's requirement to practice ownership transfer.

fn decorate(title: &mut String) {
    title.push('!');
}

fn main() {
    let mut title = String::from("Read");
    decorate(&mut title);
    println!("{title}");
}

Expected output:

Read!

main keeps ownership of the string. &mut title lends exclusive access to decorate, whose &mut String parameter lets it modify the caller's string. The binding in main needs mut to allow this mutable borrow. After the call, main can use title again. No returned string or clone is needed, and the string is dropped at the end of main.

For more practice, see Mutable borrowing.

The requirement is different here: preserve the original title while changing a second independently owned title. Complete the starter in examples/02-ownership-and-borrowing/09-hands-on/starter.rs.

fn decorate(title: String) -> String {
    todo!("Return the owned title with an exclamation mark appended")
}

fn main() {
    let original = String::from("Read Rust");
    // TODO: Make an independent snapshot before transferring original.
    let snapshot: String = todo!("Choose an explicit ownership operation");
    let updated = decorate(original);
    assert_eq!(snapshot, "Read Rust");

From the repository root:

rustc examples/02-ownership-and-borrowing/09-hands-on/starter.rs -o /tmp/rust-ownership-practice
/tmp/rust-ownership-practice

The starter deliberately panics at todo!() until completed. Success means both assertions pass and the output is:

snapshot: Read Rust, updated: Read Rust!

Explain why a clone is justified by this requirement but unnecessary in Exercise 3. Then add an empty-title case: its snapshot must remain empty and its decorated result must be !.

Solution: preserve an independent snapshot

Clone the original before moving it into decorate. The snapshot keeps its own text while the function changes the string it receives.

fn decorate(mut title: String) -> String {
    title.push('!');
    title
}

fn main() {
    let original = String::from("Read Rust");
    let snapshot = original.clone();
    let updated = decorate(original);
    assert_eq!(snapshot, "Read Rust");
    assert_eq!(updated, "Read Rust!");
    println!("snapshot: {snapshot}, updated: {updated}");

    let original = String::new();
    let snapshot = original.clone();
    let updated = decorate(original);
    assert_eq!(snapshot, "");
    assert_eq!(updated, "!");
}

decorate owns its title, appends !, and returns ownership to updated. The assertions check that the snapshot stays unchanged and the updated string contains the added punctuation, including for an empty title. The empty-title checks produce no additional output.

Unlike Exercise 3, this requirement needs two independently owned strings, so the clone is justified.

docs.title: 5. Iterate over a selected slice
docs.text:
Learn this in Topic 5: Mutable borrowing, Topic 6: Collections and iterators, and Topic 7: Slices.

A slice lets a function work on just the selected elements while the caller keeps the whole collection. The range 1..3 includes indices 1 and 2.

Complete these functions without cloning or consuming the vector:

fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    todo!("Use a for loop with iter() to sum the values")
}

fn add_one_to_each(values: &mut [i32]) {
    todo!("Use iter_mut() to increase each selected value by one")
}

fn main() {
    let mut numbers = vec![10, 20, 30, 40];
    let total = sum_values(&numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(total, 50);
    add_one_to_each(&mut numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(numbers, vec![10, 21, 31, 40]);
    println!("middle sum: {total}");
    println!("updated: {numbers:?}");
}

Save your attempt in a temporary .rs file and run it with rustc, as in Exercise 4. Then check both functions with a whole array and an empty slice: an empty sum must be 0, and updating an empty slice must do nothing. Use small numbers so addition stays within i32 limits.

Explain why *value is needed to update an element, why indices 0 and 3 remain unchanged, and why numbers remains usable after both calls. What would happen if you tried &numbers[1..5] with this four-element vector?

Solution: shared and mutable iteration 
fn sum_values(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
    let mut total = 0;
    for value in values.iter() {
        total += *value;
    }
    total
}

fn add_one_to_each(values: &mut [i32]) {
    for value in values.iter_mut() {
        *value += 1;
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut numbers = vec![10, 20, 30, 40];
    let total = sum_values(&numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(total, 50);
    add_one_to_each(&mut numbers[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(numbers, vec![10, 21, 31, 40]);
    println!("middle sum: {total}");
    println!("updated: {numbers:?}");

    let mut array = [1, 2];
    assert_eq!(sum_values(&array), 3);
    add_one_to_each(&mut array);
    assert_eq!(array, [2, 3]);

    let mut empty: [i32; 0] = [];
    assert_eq!(sum_values(&empty), 0);
    add_one_to_each(&mut empty);
    assert_eq!(empty, []);
}

iter() yields &i32; dereferencing reads the integer for the sum. iter_mut() yields &mut i32; *value += 1 changes the original element. Both functions borrow, so numbers keeps ownership. Only indices 1 and 2 are included in the mutable slice. Its borrow ends before the vector is read again. An out-of-bounds range such as 1..5 would panic.

Expected output:

middle sum: 50
updated: [10, 21, 31, 40]

After updating &mut numbers[1..3], which elements changed?

Every element, because the vector owns the slice Only elements at indices 1 and 2 Only copies, leaving the vector unchanged Check answer

docs.title: 6. Return a borrowed word
docs.text:
Learn this in Topic 4: Shared borrowing and Topic 7: Slices and text APIs.

A text slice views existing UTF-8 text. Return the first whitespace-separated word without allocating a new String. Use the split_whitespace() iterator from Topic 7: next() selects its first item, and unwrap_or("") supplies an empty result when there is no word.

fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    todo!("Return the first word, or an empty slice when there is none")
}

fn main() {
    let sentence = String::from("Rust makes borrowing useful");
    let word = first_word(&sentence);
    assert_eq!(word, "Rust");
    println!("first word: {word}");
    println!("still owned: {sentence}");
}

Run your completed program, then add assertions for "hello", "", whitespace-only text, and " café Rust". Expected results are "hello", "", "", and "café". Explain who owns the returned word's text.

Text range indices count bytes. An arbitrary byte boundary can split a UTF-8 character and cause a panic; splitting on whitespace returns valid text slices. Try inserting sentence.clear() before printing word, read the compiler error, then move the mutation after the last use of word and run again.

Solution: borrow from the input text 
fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    text.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")
}

fn main() {
    let sentence = String::from("Rust makes borrowing useful");
    let word = first_word(&sentence);
    assert_eq!(word, "Rust");
    println!("first word: {word}");
    println!("still owned: {sentence}");

    assert_eq!(first_word("hello"), "hello");
    assert_eq!(first_word(""), "");
    assert_eq!(first_word(" \t\n"), "");
    assert_eq!(first_word("  café Rust"), "café");
}

The result for a nonempty word points into the input text; no word is cloned. sentence continues to own its text. The returned reference must stay valid while used, so clearing sentence before the last use of word is rejected. After that last use, the borrow can end and clearing the string is allowed.

Expected output:

first word: Rust
still owned: Rust makes borrowing useful

Why is clearing sentence before a later use of word rejected?

Returning a slice permanently prevents all mutation first_word moved ownership out of sentence The borrowed text must remain valid until word's last use Check answer

docs.title: 7. Advanced: borrow, update, then consume titles
docs.text:
Learn this in Topic 2: Moves, Topic 5: Mutable borrowing, Topic 6: Collections and iterators, and Topic 7: Slice APIs.

Combine three access patterns in one pipeline: borrow to read, borrow mutably to edit, then take ownership to select strings for a new collection.

  • Implement mark_titles with iter_mut() to append ! to each selected title.
  • Implement total_bytes with iter() to sum the selected strings' byte lengths.
  • Implement keep_long_titles with into_iter() to consume the input vector and move titles of at least minimum_bytes into a new vector, in input order.
  • Use no clone() or to_string(). Count bytes with len(), not characters: "café" has five UTF-8 bytes and four characters.

Complete this starter:

fn mark_titles(titles: &mut [String]) {
    todo!("Append ! through mutable references")
}

fn total_bytes(titles: &[String]) -> usize {
    todo!("Sum byte lengths through shared references")
}

fn keep_long_titles(titles: Vec<String>, minimum_bytes: usize) -> Vec<String> {
    todo!("Move matching strings into a new Vec")
}

fn main() {
    let mut titles = vec![
        String::from("Read"),
        String::from("Code"),
        String::from("Test"),
        String::from("Go"),
    ];
    mark_titles(&mut titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(titles, ["Read", "Code!", "Test!", "Go"]);
    let bytes = total_bytes(&titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(bytes, 10);
    println!("selected bytes: {bytes}");
    println!("before move: {titles:?}");

    let kept = keep_long_titles(titles, 5);
    assert_eq!(kept, ["Code!", "Test!"]);
    println!("kept: {kept:?}");
}

Add assertions for empty input, no matches, a zero threshold, and a title containing "café". Predict which strings are dropped during selection and which survive in kept. Then try printing titles after the final call, explain the compiler error, and remove that invalid print.

Solution: combine all three iterator modes 
fn mark_titles(titles: &mut [String]) {
    for title in titles.iter_mut() {
        title.push('!');
    }
}

fn total_bytes(titles: &[String]) -> usize {
    let mut total = 0;
    for title in titles.iter() {
        total += title.len();
    }
    total
}

fn keep_long_titles(titles: Vec<String>, minimum_bytes: usize) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut kept = Vec::new();
    for title in titles.into_iter() {
        if title.len() >= minimum_bytes {
            kept.push(title);
        }
    }
    kept
}

fn main() {
    let mut titles = vec![
        String::from("Read"),
        String::from("Code"),
        String::from("Test"),
        String::from("Go"),
    ];
    mark_titles(&mut titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(titles, ["Read", "Code!", "Test!", "Go"]);
    let bytes = total_bytes(&titles[1..3]);
    assert_eq!(bytes, 10);
    println!("selected bytes: {bytes}");
    println!("before move: {titles:?}");

    let kept = keep_long_titles(titles, 5);
    assert_eq!(kept, ["Code!", "Test!"]);
    println!("kept: {kept:?}");

    let mut empty: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
    mark_titles(&mut empty);
    assert_eq!(total_bytes(&empty), 0);
    assert!(keep_long_titles(empty, 5).is_empty());
    assert!(keep_long_titles(vec![String::from("Go")], 5).is_empty());
    assert_eq!(keep_long_titles(vec![String::new()], 0), [""]);
    let unicode = vec![String::from("café")];
    assert_eq!(total_bytes(&unicode), 5);
    assert_eq!(keep_long_titles(unicode, 5), ["café"]);
}

The first two functions borrow slices, so the caller retains its vector. keep_long_titles takes ownership of the vector and into_iter() yields owned strings. push(title) moves each matching string into kept. Rejected strings are dropped at the end of their loop iteration. Kept strings are dropped when the returned vector is dropped.

The original titles binding is unusable after the consuming call. A new vector may allocate storage for its elements, but no string text is cloned.

Expected output:

selected bytes: 10
before move: ["Read", "Code!", "Test!", "Go"]
kept: ["Code!", "Test!"]

docs.title: Borrow without becoming the owner
docs.text:
Ownership answers “who cleans this value up?” Borrowing answers “who may use it right now?” A shared borrow, written &value, gives read-only access without creating another owner. The original variable still owns the value:

fn count_letters(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

let message = String::from("Rust");
let count = count_letters(&message); // Borrow, do not move.
println!("{message} has {count} letters");

The function receives a reference to the string slice, not the String itself. When the function returns, the borrow ends and message remains available to its owner.

The diagram is conceptual. A reference is shown as a view into owned data, not as a second owner or a literal memory address.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
What does &message create?

A second owner of the String A shared reference to the String A deep copy of the String Check answer

docs.title: Prefer &str for read-only text
docs.text:
The first version could accept &String, but &str is usually a more flexible API. A String can be viewed as a string slice, and a string literal is already a string slice:

fn count_letters(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

let owned = String::from("Rust");
let literal = "language";

println!("{}", count_letters(&owned));
println!("{}", count_letters(literal));

The function only needs to read text, so it asks for the smallest useful view instead of requiring one concrete owning type.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
Why is &str a good parameter for a read-only text function?

It takes ownership of every String It forces callers to allocate a new String It accepts borrowed text from String values and literals Check answer

docs.title: Multiple shared borrows
docs.text:
Because shared references cannot modify the value, Rust can safely allow more than one of them at the same time. This is useful when several functions need to inspect the same data:

fn first_character(text: &str) -> Option<char> {
    text.chars().next()
}

fn text_length(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.len()
}

let message = String::from("Rust");
let first = first_character(&message);
let length = text_length(&message);
println!("first: {first:?}, length: {length}");

Both calls borrow message; neither call becomes its owner. Shared borrows are read-only, so they do not conflict with each other.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
Why can two functions share &message at the same time?

Shared references are read-only Each reference becomes the owner Rust copies the entire String for every reference Check answer

docs.title: Reference lifetime and dangling prevention
docs.text:
A reference must never outlive the value it points to. Rust checks this before the program runs, so a function cannot return a reference to a local value that will be dropped when the function ends:

// This does not compile:
// fn invalid_reference() -> &String {
//     let local = String::from("temporary");
//     &local // `local` is dropped before the caller could use the reference.
// }

The safe design is to return ownership:

fn make_text() -> String {
    String::from("owned result")
}

This is the usual choice when the function creates new data: the caller owns the returned String and will clean it up.

docs.title: Alternative 1: borrow from the caller
docs.text:
If the data already belongs to the caller, return a reference tied to that input. The caller keeps the ownership, and the returned reference cannot outlive the caller's value:

fn first_word(text: &str) -> &str {
    text.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("")
}

let sentence = String::from("Rust is fast");
let word = first_word(&sentence);
println!("{word}"); // `sentence` still owns the characters.

The lifetime relationship is expressed by the function signature: the result is valid only while the borrowed input is valid.

docs.title: Alternative 2: return data with a static lifetime
docs.text:
A string literal is stored in the program's binary and is available for the whole program, so returning &'static str is safe:

fn course_name() -> &'static str {
    "Rust ownership"
}

println!("{}", course_name());

This works for fixed data, not for a String created inside the function. Adding 'static does not extend the lifetime of local variables.

docs.title: Alternative 3: return an owned heap value
docs.text:
If the result must be heap-allocated but should have one clear owner, return an owned value directly. Box<T> is useful when the value should be explicitly owned behind a pointer:

fn boxed_text() -> Box<String> {
    Box::new(String::from("owned on the heap"))
}

let text = boxed_text();
println!("{text}");

The caller owns the Box<String>, and Rust drops both the box and its String when text leaves scope. In many ordinary cases, returning String is simpler than returning Box<String>.

The compiler's rejection prevents a dangling reference from reaching runtime.

Need Prefer Create new text for the caller Return String Inspect caller-owned text Return &str tied to an input Return fixed program text Return &'static str Explicit ownership behind a pointer Return Box<String>

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
Why does invalid_reference fail to compile?

References always need to be mutable The referenced local value would be dropped before the caller used it Returning a String is never allowed Check answer

  • Binding values, ignoring fields with _ and .., and using match guards
  • Comparing a match on &TaskStatus with one that moves owned variant data
  • Choosing if let for one interesting pattern and handling other cases when needed

docs.title: 5. Option: representing missing values
docs.text:
• Some(T) and None as explicit alternatives to a missing value
  • Reading Option<T> notation without needing to define a generic type yet
  • Handling both cases with match or using if let for the present case
  • Looking up a task by position with slice or vector get; a position is not a task identifier
  • Understanding Option<&Task> as a lookup that borrows a task when present
  • Avoiding unwrap() when absence is an expected outcome

docs.title: 6. Result: representing operation outcomes
docs.text:
• Ok(T) and Err(E) as success and failure variants
  • Distinguishing an absent value from an operation that failed
  • Handling both outcomes explicitly with match
  • Returning Result<(), TaskError> from a completion method that rejects an already completed task; () means no success value
  • Leaving error propagation with ? and broader error handling for Module 5

docs.title: 7. Putting the task model together
docs.text:
• Combining the Task struct, identifier, owned title, and TaskStatus developed above
  • Using its existing methods to inspect and change status
  • Keeping status-specific data in enum variants when the model needs it
  • Storing tasks in a Vec<Task> and finding one by identifier with a simple loop that returns Option<&Task>
  • Reporting an already completed task with Result<(), TaskError>
  • Testing construction, status changes, missing tasks, and rejected operations

docs.title: Completion goal and next module
docs.text:
Model a task with a struct, status enum, and methods. Demonstrate a successful status change, a missing task through Option, and a rejected operation through Result, then explain why each outcome uses that type.

Next: Module 4: Traits and generics (planned). Encapsulation and validated API design are developed further in Module 6; borrowed structs and advanced ownership in enums return in Module 9.

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Define and construct a named-field Task struct.
  • Read and update fields while respecting ownership.
  • Use field shorthand and Debug printing.
  • Recognize when struct update syntax, tuple structs, and unit-like structs fit.

Prerequisite: Module 2: Ownership and borrowing. This lesson starts the Task example used throughout Module 3.

docs.title: A task is one value with related fields
docs.text:
A task needs an identifier and a title. Passing these as unrelated values makes it easy to mix up which title belongs to which ID. A struct gives the pair one name while keeping each field's type clear.

struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

let task = Task {
    id: 1,
    title: String::from("Read the Rust book"),
};
println!("{}: {}", task.id, task.title);

The field names are part of the type. Construction must provide both fields with the declared types. Task owns its String title. A binding must be mutable to replace a field:

let mut task = Task {
    id: 1,
    title: String::from("Read the Rust book"),
};
task.title = String::from("Practice structs");

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
Which value can construct this Task?

Task { id: 1 } Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Read") } Task { id: "1", title: "Read" } Check answer

docs.title: Field shorthand and ownership
docs.text:
When a variable has the same name as a field, write the name once. This moves the String into the struct, just as writing title: title would.

let title = String::from("Read the Rust book");
let task = Task { id: 1, title };
// println!("{title}"); // Error: title was moved into task.

Ownership reminder

String::from("Read the Rust book") creates an owned String. Assigning that value to title gives the binding ownership, and using title in Task { id: 1, title } moves that ownership into the struct. The original title binding cannot be used afterward unless you borrow or clone the string first.

Reading task.title for display borrows it for the print call. An explicit borrow can be useful when passing the field to an API that accepts &str:

println!("{}", task.title.as_str());
println!("{}", task.id); // task is still usable.

Moving the owned field into another variable is different. After a partial move, Rust still allows access to the untouched Copy field id, but the whole Task can no longer be used as a value.

let title = task.title;
println!("{title}");
println!("{}", task.id);
// println!("{}", task.title); // Error: title was moved out.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
After let task = Task { id: 1, title };, what happens to the original title: String binding?

It still owns the same String It owns an automatic clone It cannot be used because its String moved into the task Check answer

docs.title: Inspect the value with Debug
docs.text:
Add #[derive(Debug)] above the definition to print all fields while learning or diagnosing a program. {:?} uses that derived formatting behavior. Module 4 explains the trait behind it.

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

let task = Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Read") };
println!("{task:?}"); // Task { id: 1, title: "Read" }

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
What enables println!("{task:?}") for this struct?

#[derive(Debug)] on Task Making every field mutable Converting id to a String Check answer

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
This file combines construction, shorthand, mutation, borrowing, debug printing, and a partial move:

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

fn main() {
    let title = String::from("Read the Rust book");
    let mut task = Task { id: 1, title };

    println!("task: {task:?}");
    println!("title: {}", task.title.as_str());

    task.title = String::from("Practice structs");
    println!("updated: {task:?}");

    let title = task.title;
    println!("moved title: {title}");
    println!("remaining id: {}", task.id);
}

docs.title: Small extensions
docs.text:
Struct update syntax copies or moves fields from an existing value. Here the new title is supplied and id, a Copy value, comes from first:

let first = Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Read") };
let second = Task { title: String::from("Practice"), ..first };
println!("{} {}", first.id, second.title);

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
After the struct update above, which field comes from first?

Both fields Only id Only title Check answer

A tuple struct gives a value its own type without naming its fields. In TaskId(u32), the parentheses declare one field of type u32. Construct it with TaskId(1) and read its first field with .0: the zero is the field's position, while 1 is the task ID stored there. A tuple struct with two fields would use .0 and .1. Use named fields for Task, where id and title have different meanings.

struct TaskId(u32);

let id = TaskId(1);
println!("task ID: {}", id.0); // task ID: 1

A unit-like struct has no fields or stored values. For example, struct Marker; declares a type whose value can be written as Marker.

docs.text:

  2. Print the priority, then change it through a mutable Task binding.
  3. Change the title through the same binding and check the full value with Debug.
  4. Comment out let title = task.title; in the demo and compare which later uses of task become possible. Restore it afterward.

Expected result: the program compiles, prints the new priority, and still shows the updated title. A construction missing priority should produce a compiler diagnostic that points to the missing field.

docs.text:
Why is a named-field struct a good starting model for a task?

It makes all fields globally mutable It automatically stores every task in a file It groups the identifier and title with explicit names and types Check answer

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Attach methods to Task with an impl block.
  • Choose &self, &mut self, or self based on ownership needs.
  • Call methods with dot syntax.
  • Use an associated function such as Task::new to construct a value.
  • Keep a method focused on one job and return the right kind of value.

Prerequisite: Topic 1: Structs.

Refresher: a struct owns its fields

Task has an owned String field. A method can borrow that title, replace it through a mutable borrow, or move it out by consuming the whole task.

Refresher: mutability belongs to the binding

Calling a method through &mut self requires a mutable binding such as let mut task = .... The method does not make an immutable binding mutable.

docs.title: Put behavior beside the data
docs.text:
An impl block attaches functions to a type. Inside the block, the first parameter is often a receiver that describes how the method uses the value.

struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

impl Task {
    fn title(&self) -> &str {
        &self.title
    }
}

let task = Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Read") };
println!("{}", task.title());

The call task.title() is method syntax. Rust passes a reference to task as the receiver, so the method can read the field without taking ownership.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
What does &self mean in fn title(&self) -> &str?

The method consumes the task The method borrows the task for the call The method clones every field Check answer

docs.title: Choose the receiver deliberately
docs.text:
Use &self for read-only behavior. Use &mut self when the method changes a field. The caller must have a mutable binding for a mutable receiver:

impl Task {
    fn rename(&mut self, title: &str) {
        self.title = String::from(title);
    }
}

let mut task = Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Read") };
task.rename("Practice");
println!("{}", task.title);

The parameter title: &str is borrowed input. String::from(title) creates a new owned string for the field, so the task owns its title after the call.

Borrowing reminder

A borrowed &str is a temporary view. The task cannot store that view in this example, because its field is an owned String; converting with String::from gives the task its own data.

Use self when the method must take ownership. This method returns the title and consumes the task while moving the field out:

impl Task {
    fn into_title(self) -> String {
        self.title
    }
}

let task = Task { id: 1, title: String::from("Practice") };
let title = task.into_title();
println!("{title}");
// task is no longer available here: the method consumed it.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
Which declaration fits a method that replaces Task.title?

fn rename(self, title: &str) fn rename(&self, title: &str) fn rename(&mut self, title: &str) Check answer

docs.title: Associated functions construct values
docs.text:
An associated function belongs to a type but has no receiver. Task::new uses the type name and :: because it creates a task before a task exists to call a method on.

impl Task {
    fn new(id: u32, title: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            id,
            title: String::from(title),
        }
    }
}

let task = Task::new(1, "Read the Rust book");
println!("{task:?}");

Self means the type currently being implemented, here Task. The constructor accepts borrowed text and creates the owned String required by the struct.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
Why is the constructor called as Task::new(...)?

It is an associated function with no existing Task receiver It borrows every Task in the program :: always means a mutable method call Check answer

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
The demo combines an associated constructor, read-only method, mutable method, consuming method, and a focused test:

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
}

impl Task {
    /// Creates a task by taking ownership of a new title string.
    fn new(id: u32, title: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            id,
            title: String::from(title),
        }
    }

    /// Borrows the title so the task remains available to the caller.
    fn title(&self) -> &str {
        &self.title
    }

    /// Replaces the title through a mutable borrow of the task.
    fn rename(&mut self, title: &str) {
        self.title = String::from(title);
    }

    /// Consumes the task and returns its owned title.
    fn into_title(self) -> String {
        self.title
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut task = Task::new(1, "Read the Rust book");
    println!("created: {task:?} (id: {})", task.id);
    println!("title: {}", task.title());

    task.rename("Practice methods");
    println!("renamed: {task:?}");

    let title = task.into_title();
    println!("owned title: {title}");
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::Task;

    #[test]
    fn methods_read_rename_and_consume_a_task() {
        let mut task = Task::new(7, "First title");
        assert_eq!(task.id, 7);
        assert_eq!(task.title(), "First title");

        task.rename("Second title");
        assert_eq!(task.title(), "Second title");
        assert_eq!(task.into_title(), "Second title");
    }
}

/tmp/rust-task-methods

/tmp/rust-task-methods-tests

Expected program output:

title: Read the Rust book
renamed: Task { id: 1, title: "Practice methods" }
owned title: Practice methods

Use self for every method so ownership is always clear Use &self to read, &mut self to change, and self to consume Use &mut self even for methods that only print Check answer

docs.title: By the end, you will be able to
docs.text:
• Define enum types with variants and construct values of each variant.
  • Choose between unit-like, tuple-like, and struct-like variants.
  • Store different data in different variants.
  • Distinguish between "no value" and "a value of another type" using enums.
  • Use pattern matching to handle enum cases exhaustively.

Prerequisite: Topic 2: Methods and associated functions. This lesson introduces enums and extends the Task example from earlier lessons.

docs.title: What is an enum?
docs.text: An enum (enumeration) is a type that lists its possible values. Unlike C++ where enums were just integer constants, Rust enums can hold actual data and are strongly typed.

docs.title: A simple boolean alternative
docs.text:
First, consider the task status: pending, completed, or cancelled. You could use integers, but that loses clarity:

const PENDING: u8 = 1;
const COMPLETED: u8 = 2;
const CANCELLED: u8 = 3;

fn get_task_status() -> u8 { 1 }

let status = get_task_status();
// Is it PENDING? Is it COMPLETED?
if status == PENDING {
    println!("Pending");
} else if status == COMPLETED {
    println!("Completed");
} else {
    // What if it's 99?
    println!("Unknown");
}

An enum makes the alternatives explicit and forces you to handle each case:

enum TaskStatus {
    Pending,
    Completed,
    Cancelled,
}

fn get_task_status() -> TaskStatus { TaskStatus::Pending }

match get_task_status() {
    TaskStatus::Pending => println!("Pending"),
    TaskStatus::Completed => println!("Completed"),
    TaskStatus::Cancelled => println!("Cancelled"),
}

Rust will compile an error if you miss a case. This is called exhaustive matching.

docs.title: Defining an enum
docs.text:
enum TaskStatus {
    Pending,
    Completed,
    Cancelled,
}

Each possible value is a variant. The variants above are unit-like: they carry no data.

docs.title: Unit-like variants
docs.text:
Unit-like variants carry no data. They're like bool's true and false:

enum Status {
    Active,
    Inactive,
}

let s = Status::Active;

docs.title: Tuple-like variants
docs.text:
Tuple-like variants store data as a tuple:

enum Point {
    X(f64),
    Y(f64),
    Z(f64, f64),
    XY(f64, f64),
}

let x = Point::X(3.14);
let y = Point::Y(2.71);
let z = Point::Z(1.0, 2.0);
let xy = Point::XY(0.0, 1.0);

Access data with .0, .1, etc. (field positions, not names):

println!("x = {}", x.0); // x = 3.14
println!("z = {:?}", z.0, z.1);

docs.title: Struct-like variants
docs.text:
Struct-like variants store data in named fields:

struct Point3D {
    x: f64,
    y: f64,
    z: f64,
}

enum Point {
    X(Point3D),
    Y(Point3D),
    Z(Point3D),
    XY(Point3D),
}

let x = Point::X(Point3D { x: 3.14, y: 0.0, z: 0.0 });
let xy = Point::XY(Point3D { x: 0.0, y: 1.0, z: 0.0 });

Access with field names:

println!("x = {}", x.X.x); // x = 3.14
println!("xy = {:?}", xy.XY.x, xy.XY.y);

Choosing: Use unit-like for simple flags, tuple-like for ordered data without names, struct-like for named, related data.

docs.title: Representing "no value" with enums
docs.text: Consider a function that returns the first task in a list. If the list is empty, what should it return?

docs.title: Option: missing values
docs.text:
Rust provides Option<T> for "some value of type T or nothing":

let tasks: Vec<Task> = vec![];
let first = tasks.get(0); // Option<&Task>

if let Some(task) = first {
    println!("First: {}", task.title);
} else {
    println!("No first task");
}

But Option is a built-in, and sometimes you need your own enum.

docs.title: Result: success or failure
docs.text:
Consider a function that opens a file. It succeeds with the file handle, or fails with an error:

fn open_log(log_path: &str) -> Result<String, std::io::Error> {
    // Returns Ok(content) on success, Err(e) on failure
    std::fs::read_to_string(log_path)
}

let content = open_log("app.log")?; // Propagate errors with ?

Result<T, E> has two variants: Ok(T) for success and Err(E) for failure.

docs.title: Defining your own enums
docs.text:
You can define custom enums for domain-specific alternatives:

enum PaymentMethod {
    CreditCard(String), // card number as String
    BankTransfer(f64),  // amount as f64
    Crypto(String, f64), // coin and amount
}

fn process_payment(method: &str, amount: f64) -> PaymentMethod {
    match method {
        "credit" => PaymentMethod::CreditCard(String::from("4242")),
        "bank" => PaymentMethod::BankTransfer(amount),
        "crypto" => PaymentMethod::Crypto(String::from("BTC"), amount),
        _ => panic!("Unsupported payment method"),
    }
}

let payment = process_payment("crypto", 100.0);
match payment {
    PaymentMethod::CreditCard(card) => println!("Card: {}", card),
    PaymentMethod::BankTransfer(amount) => println!("Transfer: {}", amount),
    PaymentMethod::Crypto(coin, amt) => println!("{}: {}", coin, amt),
}

Each variant can carry different data types, making the type system enforce correctness.

docs.title: Pattern matching with enums
docs.text: Pattern matching (match) is the primary way to handle enums.

docs.title: Exhaustive matching
docs.text:
Rust requires all cases to be covered:

enum Status {
    Active,
    Inactive,
}

let s = Status::Active;

match s {
    Status::Active => println!("Active"),
    Status::Inactive => println!("Inactive"),
    // Missing case! Compiler error.
}

docs.title: Ignoring cases with _
docs.text:
Use _ to handle "any other case":

enum Operation {
    Add(f64, f64),
    Subtract(f64, f64),
    Multiply(f64, f64),
    Divide(f64, f64),
}

let op = Operation::Add(1.0, 2.0);

match op {
    Operation::Add(a, b) => println!("{}", a + b),
    Operation::Subtract(a, b) => println!("{}", a - b),
    Operation::Multiply(a, b) => println!("{}", a * b),
    Operation::Divide(a, b) => println!("{}", a / b),
    Operation::Other => println!("Unknown operation"),
}

docs.title: Partial destructuring with ..
docs.text:
Ignore all fields except some:

enum Status {
    Active,
    Inactive,
    Archived { created_at: u64, user_id: u64 },
}

let s = Status::Archived { created_at: 123, user_id: 456 };

match s {
    Status::Archived { created_at, .. } => println!("Created: {}", created_at),
    Status::Active | Status::Inactive => println!("Active or inactive"),
}

docs.title: Match guards
docs.text:
Add conditions with if:

enum TaskStatus {
    Completed,
    Pending,
    Cancelled,
}

let status = TaskStatus::Completed;

match status {
    TaskStatus::Completed if status == TaskStatus::Completed => println!("Completed"),
    TaskStatus::Pending => println!("Pending"),
    TaskStatus::Cancelled => println!("Cancelled"),
}

docs.title: If let for single cases
docs.text:
Use if let for "only this case, ignore others":

enum TaskStatus {
    Completed,
    Pending,
    Cancelled,
}

let status = TaskStatus::Completed;

if let TaskStatus::Completed = status {
    println!("Task completed!");
} // Pending and Cancelled are ignored

docs.title: Extending the Task model with TaskStatus
docs.text:
Now we extend the Task struct with a status enum.

enum TaskStatus {
    Pending,
    Completed,
    Cancelled,
}

struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
    status: TaskStatus,
}

let task = Task {
    id: 1,
    title: String::from("Read the Rust book"),
    status: TaskStatus::Pending,
};

match task.status {
    TaskStatus::Pending => println!("Pending"),
    TaskStatus::Completed => println!("Completed"),
    TaskStatus::Cancelled => println!("Cancelled"),
}

docs.title: Adding methods that change status
docs.text:
impl Task {
    fn complete(&mut self) {
        self.status = TaskStatus::Completed;
    }

    fn cancel(&mut self) {
        self.status = TaskStatus::Cancelled;
    }
}

let mut task = Task {
    id: 1,
    title: String::from("Read the Rust book"),
    status: TaskStatus::Pending,
};

task.complete();
match task.status {
    TaskStatus::Pending => println!("Pending"),
    TaskStatus::Completed => println!("Completed"),
    TaskStatus::Cancelled => println!("Cancelled"),
}

docs.title: Complete runnable example
docs.text:
//! Example: Rust enums with variants, pattern matching, and the Task model.

struct Task {
    id: u32,
    title: String,
    status: TaskStatus,
}

enum TaskStatus {
    Pending,
    Completed,
    Cancelled,
}

impl Task {
    fn new(id: u32, title: String) -> Self {
        Task {
            id,
            title,
            status: TaskStatus::Pending,
        }
    }

    fn complete(&mut self) {
        self.status = TaskStatus::Completed;
    }

    fn cancel(&mut self) {
        self.status = TaskStatus::Cancelled;
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("Created task: Task {{ id: 1, title: \"Read the Rust book\", status: Pending }}");

    let mut task = Task::new(1, String::from("Read the Rust book"));

    match &task.status {
        TaskStatus::Pending => println!("Status: Pending"),
        TaskStatus::Completed => println!("Status: Completed"),
        TaskStatus::Cancelled => println!("Status: Cancelled"),
    }

    task.complete();
    println!("Completed!");

    match &task.status {
        TaskStatus::Pending => println!("Status: Pending"),
        TaskStatus::Completed => println!("Status: Completed"),
        TaskStatus::Cancelled => println!("Status: Cancelled"),
    }
}

docs.text:
1. Add data to TaskStatus: Create a variant Completed { description: String } that stores additional information about what was completed. Update all matching code and the runnable example.

  2. Add a payment method enum: Define a PaymentMethod enum with variants for credit card, bank transfer, and crypto. Create a function that returns the appropriate variant based on input.

  3. Pattern matching practice: Write a function that takes a custom enum with multiple variants and returns a descriptive string for each case, using pattern matching.

  4. Combine with Option: Create an enum TaskResult that can be Pending, Completed, or None (using None or a custom variant). Write code that handles all three cases.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Enums represent discrete alternatives: enum Status { Pending, Completed, Cancelled }
  • Variants can be unit-like, tuple-like, or struct-like, storing different data
  • Pattern matching with match handles all enum cases; Rust enforces exhaustiveness
  • Use Option<T> for "missing values" and Result<T, E> for "success/failure"
  • Custom enums provide clear, type-safe alternatives for domain-specific needs
  • Struct-like variants with named fields offer the clearest representation for complex data
